title.raw: Cycling Flanders: Kwaremont, Paterberg and the Tour of Flanders Roads
title.rendered: Cycling Flanders: Kwaremont, Paterberg and the Tour of Flanders Roads

content.raw:
The Ronde van Vlaanderen is one of the five Monuments of cycling, and the roads it uses are open to you all year: short, savage climbs, rough cobbles and quiet farm lanes that link them together. If you want to ride the roads you have watched on television every spring, Flanders is the most direct way to do it.

This guide covers the climbs and cobbled sectors that matter, a classic loop around Oudenaarde, when to go, and the practical details that make a Flanders trip run smoothly.

Why ride Flanders

Three things set Flanders apart from the mountain regions:

  • The Ronde is a living route. The climbs and cobbled sectors are public roads. You ride the same hills the pros race, in the same wheel tracks, often within a few kilometres of each other.
  • Short, sharp effort. There are no 20 km passes here. The climbs are brief, steep and repeated, which makes Flanders a different kind of hard from the Alps or the Dolomites.
  • Cycling culture everywhere. Cafés, museums and village squares are built around the sport. Race weekend in early April is among the best atmospheres in cycling.

The climbs that matter

Oude Kwaremont

The cobbled climb that defines the Ronde, and the one to ride first. It is around 2 km long with roughly 1.5 km of cobbles, and the gradient is moderate rather than brutal. The challenge is the surface: the stones shake you for minutes, so relax your grip, stay seated and keep your cadence smooth.

Paterberg

Short and ferocious. The Paterberg is only a few hundred metres, but it is steep from the first pedal stroke, with the cobbles at their most punishing near the top. Pick your gear before you reach the base, because there is no time to change halfway up.

Koppenberg

One of the most feared climbs in Belgium. Narrow, steep and cobbled, the Koppenberg is where a missed line or a rider stopping in front of you can end your climb. Ride it early in the day, when the road is clear, and keep your weight over the rear wheel.

Muur van Geraardsbergen

The Muur is a short cobbled ramp leading to a small chapel at the top, and one of the most iconic climbs in the sport. The reward at the summit is the view over the town and a place in cycling history.

A classic Flanders loop

A route most riders enjoy: start in Oudenaarde, link the Oude Kwaremont and Paterberg, add the Koppenberg and Taaienberg, then climb the Muur and return through the Flemish Ardennes. Depending on the variations you choose, this runs roughly 100 to 130 km with a cluster of short climbs and several cobbled sectors, which is a demanding day even for strong riders. For a gentler outing, ride a shorter loop of 60 to 70 km that takes in the Kwaremont and Paterberg only.

When to go

  • Late March to early April: race season, with the Ronde itself in early April. The atmosphere is unmatched, but the weather is cold and changeable and accommodation fills up early.
  • May to June: the best balance of mild temperatures, long days and quieter roads.
  • July and August: warm and settled, with the lowest chance of rain on the cobbles.
  • September and October: autumn colours and cooler air, with more wet days.
  • November to February: possible on dry days, but expect cold, wind and slippery stones.

Practical tips

  • Tyres: choose wider tyres, ideally 28 to 32 mm, and run them softer than you would on smooth tarmac. It makes the cobbles far more comfortable and more controlled.
  • Weather: Flanders is flat and exposed. Wind and rain are normal, so carry a rain jacket even when the forecast looks good.
  • Wet cobbles: treat them with respect. Brake before the stones, not on them, and avoid the polished edges and the gutter.
  • Race weekend: the Ronde cyclosportive is held the day before the pro race. Roads and hotels are very busy, so book early.
  • Getting there: Brussels Airport is the closest major hub, and trains connect Brussels to Ghent in under an hour. Oudenaarde, Ghent and Bruges all make good bases.
  • Don't skip the museum: the Tour of Flanders Centre in Oudenaarde is worth an hour on a rest day.

The climbs and cobbled roads in this guide are the heart of our Tour of Flanders Experience, a 4-night, 5-day trip on Ronde weekend (1–5 April 2027). You ride the legendary climbs in the We Ride Flanders sportive, then watch the pros race the same roads the next day with premium race access. The route, hotel and support are organised for you.

Prefer to ride Flanders with your own club or friends? Talk to us about a custom tour and we will build it around your dates and fitness.

Frequently asked questions

Is Flanders good for cycling?
Yes. It combines famous climbs, cobbled sectors, racing history and a dense network of quiet roads, which makes it one of the most rewarding road cycling destinations in Europe.

How hard is the Oude Kwaremont?
It is long for a Flanders climb, but the gradient is moderate. The cobbles make it tiring rather than steep, and most fit riders can ride it comfortably at their own pace.

How hard are the Paterberg and Koppenberg?
Very hard. Both are short but steep, with rough cobbles, so they need low gearing, good balance and fresh legs.

What is the best month to cycle in Flanders?
May, June and September are usually the best, with comfortable temperatures. Early April is best if you want the Ronde atmosphere and can accept cold weather.

title.raw: Cycling Lake Como: Ghisallo, Sormano and the Giro di Lombardia Roads
title.rendered: Cycling Lake Como: Ghisallo, Sormano and the Giro di Lombardia Roads

content.raw:
The roads around the lake carry the history of the Giro di Lombardia, the Madonna del Ghisallo chapel is the spiritual home of every cyclist, and the climbs are close enough together that you can ride several of them in one day. If you want Italian racing roads without the Dolomites' altitude or the Stelvio's weather risk, Como is one of the best places to start.

This guide covers the climbs worth riding, a classic loop, when to go, and the practical details that make a week here run smoothly.

Why ride Lake Como

Three things set Como apart from other Italian cycling regions:

  • Racing history on every road. The Giro di Lombardia, the "race of the falling leaves", has crossed these hills for over a century. You ride the same climbs the pros do.
  • Compact geography. Most of the best climbs sit within an hour of each other. You can base yourself in one hotel and ride something different every day.
  • A long season. Spring and autumn are excellent, and the lake keeps temperatures mild when the mountains further north are still snowed in.

The climbs that matter

Madonna del Ghisallo

The most famous climb on the lake, and the one to ride first. From Bellagio it is roughly 10 km at a steady, rhythmic gradient that rewards pacing rather than power. At the top is the small chapel where cyclists are honoured as under the protection of Our Lady of Ghisallo, and next to it the cycling museum, full of bikes, jerseys and photographs from the sport's history. Allow time to stop. The climb is the warm-up; the summit is the point.

Muro di Sormano

The opposite character: short, brutal and famous. The Muro di Sormano is under 2 km but averages around 17% with ramps well beyond 20%. It was used in the Giro di Lombardia in 2012 and remains one of Italy's toughest climbs per kilometre. Gear down, stay seated, and do not start it unless your legs are fresh. If you want the climb without the Muro, the approach via the alternative road is far gentler.

Civiglio and the Como side

Above the city of Como, the roads to Civiglio, San Fermo della Battaglia and Brunate give you short, steep, technical climbs with lake views. They are ideal for a half-day ride or as the opening and closing sections of a longer loop.

Val d'Intelvi

The quieter western side of the lake. Longer, more gradual climbs, far less traffic, and a good option on days when the main lakeside road is busy.

A classic Como loop

A route most riders enjoy: start in Como, ride along the lake to Bellagio, climb Madonna del Ghisallo, descend toward the Lecco side and return via the Brianza hills. Depending on the variations you choose, this runs roughly 90 to 110 km with 1,500 to 2,000 m of climbing, which is a full day but well within reach for a fit club rider. Add the Muro di Sormano only if you want a serious challenge.

When to go

  • April to June: the best balance of mild temperatures, green hills and manageable traffic.
  • July and August: hot, busy and very popular with tourists. Ride early.
  • September and October: settled weather, autumn colours and the Lombardia season atmosphere.
  • November to March: possible on good days, but expect cold mornings and shorter daylight.

Practical tips

  • Traffic: the lakeside roads can be busy, especially on weekends and in summer. Plan to leave the shore early and head uphill, where roads are quieter.
  • Tunnels: the lake roads include several tunnels. Lights front and back are not optional.
  • Gearing: a compact chainset and a wide cassette will make Ghisallo comfortable and Sormano possible.
  • Water and food: villages are frequent, but plan your stops before the longer climbs.
  • Getting there: Milan's airports and Milan Centrale station both connect to Como and Lecco in around an hour.

Lake Como and the Lombardy climbs in this guide are the heart of our Lombardia cycling tour. You ride them guided by our team, with the route, hotel and support organised for you and the daily distance matched to the group.

Prefer to ride Como with your own club or friends? Talk to us about a custom tour and we will build it around your dates and fitness.

Frequently asked questions

Is Lake Como good for cycling?
Yes. It combines famous climbs, racing history, scenic roads and an easy-to-reach base, which makes it one of the most rewarding road cycling destinations in northern Italy.

How hard is Madonna del Ghisallo?
It is a long, steady climb of roughly 10 km from Bellagio, not a steep one. Most fit riders can ride it comfortably at their own pace.

How hard is Madonna del Ghisallo?
Very hard. It is short but averages around 17% with sections much steeper, so it needs low gearing and good legs.

What is the best month to cycle Lake Como?
May, June, September and early October are usually the best, with comfortable temperatures and good riding conditions.

title.raw: What to Pack for a Gravel Cycling Tour
title.rendered: What to Pack for a Gravel Cycling Tour

content.raw:
The roads are rougher, the support points are further apart, the weather changes faster on exposed tracks, and a mechanical that would be a five-minute roadside fix on tarmac can turn into a long walk on a remote gravel sector. After guiding gravel tours across Tuscany, Cyprus, Slovenia, Sardinia, Sicily and beyond, here's what I actually tell riders to bring — and what to leave at home.

Bike Setup and Tires

This is where most first-time gravel travellers get it wrong before they've even packed a bag.

  • Bring a spare tire, not just a tube. Sidewall cuts happen more often on gravel than on road, and a tube alone won't fix a torn casing. A lightweight folding spare packs down small and has saved more than one trip I've guided.
  • Tire width and tread matter more than anything else you'll pack. For mixed gravel and tarmac routes, 40-45mm with a light tread is usually the sweet spot — wide enough to handle loose surfaces and washboard gravel, narrow enough to stay efficient on the paved connector sections most routes include. For tours with genuinely rougher sections, go up to 50mm if your frame clearance allows it — check with your tour operator in advance if you're unsure what a specific route calls for.
  • Tubeless setup is close to essential. Sealant handles the small punctures that gravel throws at you constantly — thorns, sharp stones, sidewall nicks — without forcing a roadside tube change every time. If you're not already running tubeless, it's worth converting before you travel, not on your first morning on strade bianche.

The Repair Kit: Built for Being Further From Help

On a road tour, you're rarely more than a short ride from a village or a passing car. On gravel, especially through Tuscany's white roads or Sardinia's interior, that's often not true — so the kit needs to assume you're on your own for longer.

  • Tubeless plug kit plus a couple of spare tubes, in case sealant alone can't close the gap and you need to convert back to a tube mid-route.
  • A small top-up bottle of spare sealant. Sealant dries out over the course of a long, hot day, and if you do need to change a tire halfway through a multi-day trip, having a top-up on hand means you're not stuck relying on a dry system.
  • A multi-tool with a chain breaker. Gravel's rougher terrain is harder on drivetrains than smooth tarmac, and a snapped chain in the middle of nowhere is a very different problem than one on a quiet backroad.
  • A mini electric pump. These have genuinely changed the game for gravel travel — reseating a tubeless tire by hand with a mini pump on the roadside is a real struggle, and an electric one does it in seconds without the arm workout. Worth the extra weight in the saddle bag.
  • Spare brake pads. Before going on a gravel tour is always recommended to change your brake pads and have fresh new pads for the long descents ahead. However is essential to have a spare set just in case you end up using them all.
  • A small bottle of chain oil. Dust is constant on gravel, and it dries a chain out far faster than road riding does — a dry, gritty chain both wears faster and rides worse. A quick drip at the end of each day keeps the drivetrain running properly for the rest of the trip.
  • Zip ties and a small roll of tape. Unglamorous, but they fix more improvised problems on gravel — a loose fender, a rattling bag, a cracked mudguard — than any single specialist tool.

Clothing: Layering for Exposed, Changeable Terrain

Gravel routes spend more time away from towns and tree cover than road routes typically do, which means more direct exposure to sun, wind, and sudden weather shifts — especially at altitude or on exposed ridgelines.

  • Eye protection with a clear or light lens option. Dust kicked up on dry gravel is a real nuisance, and riding without eye protection through it isn't pleasant for long.
  • A lightweight, packable gilet or wind vest, even in summer. Gravel routes often climb into more exposed terrain than the equivalent road route nearby, and conditions change fast once you're out of the valley.
  • Bib shorts with a chamois built for longer days in the saddle. Rougher terrain means more time out of a smooth pedal stroke and more vibration through the saddle — a well-broken-in chamois matters more here than on road.
  • Gloves with real padding. Sustained vibration from washboard gravel and loose stone is genuinely fatiguing on the hands over a multi-day trip, far more than most riders expect coming from road cycling.

Navigation and Safety

Gravel routes frequently run through areas with patchy signal and unmarked junctions, which changes what "being prepared" means.

  • A GPS device or phone mount with the route pre-loaded, and don't rely on signal alone — download offline maps for the region before you travel.
  • A small battery pack. Longer days off the beaten track mean longer stretches between charging opportunities, and a dead GPS at a junction in the middle of nowhere is not where you want to be improvising.
  • Basic first aid essentials. Falls on loose gravel are more common than on tarmac, and being a genuine distance from help changes the calculation on what's worth carrying.

Bags: What to Bring It All In

If your trip includes point-to-point riding or overnight stops away from your base, check with your tour operator whether luggage is transferred for you — on our guided gravel trips it is, which means you can pack lighter on the bike itself and save the bikepacking setup for routes where it's genuinely needed.

  • A saddle bag or half-frame bag for tools and repair kit, keeping weight low and central rather than in a backpack, which gets uncomfortable fast on rough terrain.
  • A small handlebar bag or top-tube bag for anything you need quick access to — nutrition, phone, gloves — without stopping to dig through a saddle bag.

Nutrition and Hydration for Longer, Remoter Stretches

  • Carry more than you think you need. Gravel routes often have longer gaps between towns, cafés, and water sources than the equivalent road route, and running low on a remote stretch is a much bigger problem than on a well-serviced road ride.
  • Go with 750ml bidons over 500ml. With longer gaps between refill points, the extra capacity matters — two 750ml bottles buy noticeably more margin than two 500ml ones for the same number of cages.
  • A backup water filter or purification tablets, if your route includes genuinely remote sections — not always necessary, but worth checking against your specific itinerary.

The One Thing Riders Consistently Forget

A pre-trip shakedown ride on similar terrain, in the actual kit you're planning to bring. Tire pressure that feels fine in a car park often isn't right on real gravel, and a saddle bag that seemed secure in the shop can rattle loose after two hours of washboard track. If you're joining one of our gravel cycling tours, we'll always run through your setup before the first big day — but the more of this you've already dialled in beforehand, the more of the trip you get to actually enjoy.

For general trip-packing advice beyond gravel-specific gear — documents, packing lists for flights, bike transport — our guide to packing for a European cycling holiday covers the broader basics.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a dedicated gravel bike, or can I use my road bike? It depends on the route. However in all of our Gravel Bike Tours, a gravel bike is must.

Is tubeless really necessary for a gravel tour? Not strictly, but it's strongly recommended. Punctures are simply more frequent on gravel, and sealant resolves most of them without stopping. Riders on tubes should carry more spares than they would for a road trip.

How much should I pack for a multi-day gravel tour? Less than you think, if your tour includes luggage transfer between stops — in that case, pack light for the bike itself (repair kit, nutrition, layers) and let your main bag travel separately. If you're bikepacking unsupported, that changes the calculation significantly.

What's the biggest packing mistake you see? Under-preparing the repair kit. Riders often pack road-trip repair basics — one tube, a multi-tool — and then face a sidewall cut or a tubeless issue gravel is simply more prone to, with no backup plan.

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours

  • Tubeless setup is close to essential. The Repair Kit: Built for Being Further From Help

On a road tour, you’re rarely more than a short ride from a village or a passing car. On gravel, especially through Tuscany’s white roads or Sardinia’s interior, that’s often not true — so the kit needs to assume you’re on your own for longer.

  • Tubeless plug kit plus a couple of spare tubes, in case sealant alone can’t close the gap and you need to convert back to a tube mid-route.
  • A small top-up bottle of spare sealant. Sealant dries out over the course of a long, hot day, and if you do need to change a tire halfway through a multi-day trip, having a top-up on hand means you’re not stuck relying on a dry system.
  • A multi-tool with a chain breaker. Gravel’s rougher terrain is harder on drivetrains than smooth tarmac, and a snapped chain in the middle of nowhere is a very different problem than one on a quiet backroad.
  • A mini electric pump. These have genuinely changed the game for gravel travel — reseating a tubeless tire by hand with a mini pump on the roadside is a real struggle, and an electric one does it in seconds without the arm workout. Worth the extra weight in the saddle bag.
  • Spare brake pads. Before going on a gravel tour is always recommended to change your brake pads and have fresh new pads for the long descents ahead. However is essential to have a spare set just in case you end up using them all.
  • A small bottle of chain oil. Dust is constant on gravel, and it dries a chain out far faster than road riding does — a dry, gritty chain both wears faster and rides worse. A quick drip at the end of each day keeps the drivetrain running properly for the rest of the trip.
  • Zip ties and a small roll of tape. Unglamorous, but they fix more improvised problems on gravel — a loose fender, a rattling bag, a cracked mudguard — than any single specialist tool.

Clothing: Layering for Exposed, Changeable Terrain

Gravel routes spend more time away from towns and tree cover than road routes typically do, which means more direct exposure to sun, wind, and sudden weather shifts — especially at altitude or on exposed ridgelines.

  • Eye protection with a clear or light lens option. Dust kicked up on dry gravel is a real nuisance, and riding without eye protection through it isn’t pleasant for long.
  • A lightweight, packable gilet or wind vest, even in summer. Gravel routes often climb into more exposed terrain than the equivalent road route nearby, and conditions change fast once you’re out of the valley.
  • Bib shorts with a chamois built for longer days in the saddle. Rougher terrain means more time out of a smooth pedal stroke and more vibration through the saddle — a well-broken-in chamois matters more here than on road.
  • Gloves with real padding. Sustained vibration from washboard gravel and loose stone is genuinely fatiguing on the hands over a multi-day trip, far more than most riders expect coming from road cycling.

Navigation and Safety

Gravel routes frequently run through areas with patchy signal and unmarked junctions, which changes what “being prepared” means.

  • A GPS device or phone mount with the route pre-loaded, and don’t rely on signal alone — download offline maps for the region before you travel.
  • A small battery pack. Longer days off the beaten track mean longer stretches between charging opportunities, and a dead GPS at a junction in the middle of nowhere is not where you want to be improvising.
  • Basic first aid essentials. Falls on loose gravel are more common than on tarmac, and being a genuine distance from help changes the calculation on what’s worth carrying.

Bags: What to Bring It All In

If your trip includes point-to-point riding or overnight stops away from your base, check with your tour operator whether luggage is transferred for you — on our guided gravel trips it is, which means you can pack lighter on the bike itself and save the bikepacking setup for routes where it’s genuinely needed.

  • A saddle bag or half-frame bag for tools and repair kit, keeping weight low and central rather than in a backpack, which gets uncomfortable fast on rough terrain.
  • A small handlebar bag or top-tube bag for anything you need quick access to — nutrition, phone, gloves — without stopping to dig through a saddle bag.

Nutrition and Hydration for Longer, Remoter Stretches

  • Carry more than you think you need. Gravel routes often have longer gaps between towns, cafés, and water sources than the equivalent road route, and running low on a remote stretch is a much bigger problem than on a well-serviced road ride.
  • Go with 750ml bidons over 500ml. With longer gaps between refill points, the extra capacity matters — two 750ml bottles buy noticeably more margin than two 500ml ones for the same number of cages.
  • A backup water filter or purification tablets, if your route includes genuinely remote sections — not always necessary, but worth checking against your specific itinerary.

The One Thing Riders Consistently Forget

A pre-trip shakedown ride on similar terrain, in the actual kit you’re planning to bring. Tire pressure that feels fine in a car park often isn’t right on real gravel, and a saddle bag that seemed secure in the shop can rattle loose after two hours of washboard track. If you’re joining one of our gravel cycling tours, we’ll always run through your setup before the first big day — but the more of this you’ve already dialled in beforehand, the more of the trip you get to actually enjoy.

For general trip-packing advice beyond gravel-specific gear — documents, packing lists for flights, bike transport — our guide to packing for a European cycling holiday covers the broader basics.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a dedicated gravel bike, or can I use my road bike? It depends on the route. However in all of our Gravel Bike Tours, a gravel bike is must.

Is tubeless really necessary for a gravel tour? Not strictly, but it’s strongly recommended. Punctures are simply more frequent on gravel, and sealant resolves most of them without stopping. Riders on tubes should carry more spares than they would for a road trip.

How much should I pack for a multi-day gravel tour? Less than you think, if your tour includes luggage transfer between stops — in that case, pack light for the bike itself (repair kit, nutrition, layers) and let your main bag travel separately. If you’re bikepacking unsupported, that changes the calculation significantly.

What’s the biggest packing mistake you see? Under-preparing the repair kit. Riders often pack road-trip repair basics — one tube, a multi-tool — and then face a sidewall cut or a tubeless issue gravel is simply more prone to, with no backup plan.

— Matteo Cigala

title.rendered: Cycling the Stelvio Pass: Complete Guide

content.raw:
If you ride bikes, you already know the name. The Passo dello Stelvio isn't just Italy's greatest climb — it's one of the defining ascents in all of cycling, a fixture of the Giro d'Italia since 1953, and a rite of passage for anyone serious about riding mountains. I've climbed it more times than I can count, both racing and guiding, and it still gets my heart rate up before I even clip in.

This guide covers everything I'd want to know before attempting it for the first time: the numbers, the route options, the weather risks, and the small details that make the difference between a miserable slog and one of the best days you'll ever have on a bike.

A Quick History

The Stelvio was built in the 1820s under Habsburg rule, originally as a military and trade road connecting Lombardy to the rest of the Austrian Empire — which is part of why the engineering is so remarkable for its age. It has featured in the Giro d'Italia more than a dozen times, and the "Cima Coppi" — the award given to the highest point reached in that year's race — is awarded here more often than at any other climb. Fausto Coppi, Marco Pantani, and countless other legends of the sport have all suffered up these switchbacks, and riding it yourself puts you directly into that history.

Stelvio Pass: The Key Numbers

  • Elevation at summit: 2,758m — the second-highest paved pass in the Alps, and the highest in Italy
  • Classic ascent (from Prato allo Stelvio): 24.3km, average gradient 7.4%, 1,808m of climbing
  • Hairpin bends: 48 numbered switchbacks on the Prato side alone, each marked with a small stone signpost counting down to the summit
  • Ride time: 1.5–3 hours depending on fitness, most riders average around 2 hours
  • Steepest sections: ramps touching 12% in the upper third, though the climb rarely sustains anything that steep for long

Those numbers don't really tell the story, though. The Stelvio is less about any single steep ramp and more about sustained rhythm — you settle into a gear, find a cadence, and just stay there for two hours while the valley drops away beneath you and the switchbacks stack up below like a drawn diagram.

Which Side Should You Climb?

There are three genuinely different approaches, and each has its own character.

From Prato allo Stelvio (the Bormio-side numbering, climbing north) — this is the classic, most photographed route, with the tightly stacked hairpins visible from below that appear in every cycling documentary and calendar. The gradient here is remarkably consistent, which actually makes pacing easier than you'd expect from the visuals.

From Bormio — slightly longer at around 21km, with a similar average gradient but a different rhythm — more exposed in sections, and in my experience the quieter option if you want fewer cars and tour buses sharing the road with you.

From Switzerland via the Umbrail Pass — a partially unpaved option for the more adventurous rider, joining the main Stelvio road near the summit. This is a good option if you're already riding a gravel bike or want to avoid the busiest tourist stretch entirely.

If it's your first time, ride the Prato side. It's the one worth doing once purely for the scenery and the sense of occasion, and the gradient is honest and consistent rather than punishing in sudden surges — which makes it more approachable for a strong recreational rider than the raw numbers might suggest.

Best Time to Ride

The pass is only open roughly late May or early June through October — it's closed under snow the rest of the year, and even once open, you'll often find snow banks taller than a person stacked at the roadside near the summit in early June. This is actually part of the spectacle; riding through a narrow corridor of snow at 2,700m in shorts and a jersey is one of those strange, memorable cycling experiences.

July and August give you the most reliable, settled weather, but also the most traffic and tour groups — motorbikes in particular tend to treat the hairpins as a playground, so stay alert on the outside of blind corners. If you can manage it, aim for mid-June or September instead: cooler mornings, noticeably thinner crowds, and long stretches of road entirely to yourself.

Start early, ideally before 9am. Not just for the sunrise light on the switchbacks, which is genuinely spectacular and worth planning a photo stop for, but because afternoon thunderstorms build quickly in this part of the Alps in summer, and you do not want to be exposed above the treeline when one arrives. Lightning at 2,700m is not a risk worth taking for a better lunch view.

What to Bring

Sunscreen reapplied before the descent — UV at altitude is stronger than it feels, especially with the wind cooling your skin

A packable jacket, not just a gilet — it can be 15-20°C colder at the summit than in the valley, and you'll be descending at 50km/h+ afterward, which turns any temperature gap into a genuinely cold experience

Full-finger gloves for the descent, even in summer

Enough water for 2+ hours of steady effort — there are a couple of refreshment stops near the top in season, but don't rely on them being open

A compact or triple chainset if you're not used to sustained climbing — there's no shame in an easier gear here; the goal is rhythm, not heroics, and grinding a harder gear for two hours will wreck your legs for the rest of your trip

Common Mistakes First-Timers Make

The single biggest mistake is going out too hard on the lower slopes. The gradient near the bottom feels almost gentle compared to what's coming, and it's tempting to ride at a pace that feels sustainable for the first 20 minutes — but the effort compounds, and riders who hammer the early kilometres are often the ones walking sections near the top. Treat the whole climb as a two-hour time trial against yourself, not a series of short efforts.

The second mistake is underestimating the descent. After two hours of climbing, it's tempting to let gravity do the work and bomb down the other side — but the road surface, blind hairpins, and shared traffic with cars, motorbikes, and other cyclists mean a controlled, confident descent beats a fast, reckless one every time.

The Stelvio Gravel Route

Most cyclists know the Stelvio for its legendary 48 hairpins, but there's another way to experience this iconic mountain—one that is quieter, wilder, and arguably even more memorable.

The Stelvio Gravel route leaves the main road before the summit and follows a military gravel road high above the valley. The climb becomes less about counting hairpins and more about riding through a spectacular alpine landscape, with panoramic views over the Ortler massif and the famous switchbacks far below.

The gravel itself is not highly technical, making it accessible to anyone with a gravel bike or a mountain bike and a reasonable level of fitness. The challenge comes from the altitude and the sustained climbing rather than difficult terrain. As with the road ascent, you'll be riding above 2,500 metres, so pacing yourself is essential.

One of the biggest advantages of the gravel route is the solitude. While the main Stelvio road can be busy during the summer months, the gravel alternative feels remote and peaceful. It's common to ride for long stretches without seeing another cyclist, making it a completely different experience from the classic ascent.

On our tours, we often offer the Stelvio Gravel as an optional route for riders looking for something different. Those who prefer the traditional road climb can tackle the famous hairpins, while more adventurous riders can head onto the gravel before both groups meet again later in the day.

If you've already ridden the classic Stelvio, the gravel route offers a fresh perspective on one of cycling's most iconic mountains—and for many riders, it becomes the highlight of the entire trip.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

There are two ways to ride the Stelvio with us. Our Italian Alps trip includes the Stelvio as part of the core itinerary — it's one of the signature climbs of that week. Alternatively, if you're joining our Lake Garda cycling tour in September, the Stelvio is also offered as an optional day trip from our Garda base, with a full support vehicle following the group so you're never riding it unsupported, and a van waiting at the top for anyone who wants a lift back down rather than descending.

I lead this climb personally a lot of weeks in season, and it never gets old watching someone reach the top for the first time — the summit sign at 2,758m gets more photos taken next to it than almost anywhere else we visit.

If you're building toward this one, don't underestimate it — it rewards preparation more than raw power. Get consistent time in the saddle and some sustained climbing practice a few weeks out, and the Stelvio will be one of the best days you've ever had on a bike.

If you'd like a different combination of climbs or timing than either standard itinerary offers, we're also happy to design a fully custom tour around the Stelvio for your group.

Frequently Asked Questions

How fit do I need to be to ride the Stelvio?
A rider comfortable sustaining a moderate effort for 1.5–3 hours can complete it. You don't need racing fitness, but consistent time in the saddle in the weeks before your trip makes a significant difference to how much you enjoy it.

Is the Stelvio suitable for e-bikes?
Yes, and it's an increasingly popular way to tackle it. The consistent gradient works well with e-bike assistance, and several of our guests have ridden it this way with excellent results.

How busy is the road in summer?
Reasonably busy in July and August, with cars, motorbikes, and tour buses sharing the road, especially near the top where there's a small hub of cafés and souvenir stands. June and September are noticeably quieter.

Can I ride the Stelvio without a guided tour?
Absolutely — it's a public road open to all cyclists in season. A guided day gives you support vehicle backup, local knowledge of the quieter timing windows, and someone who knows exactly where to stop for the best views and photos.

Should I follow a training plan to get ready for the Stelvio?
Yes! While you don't need a training plan to complete the Stelvio, being well-prepared will make the climbs much more enjoyable and help you get the most from the tour.
If you'd like personalised coaching before your trip, check out my coaching plans here: coaching.cigalacycling.com.

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours

title.raw: Best Time to Ride the Dolomites
title.rendered: Best Time to Ride the Dolomites

content.raw:
I get asked this more than almost any other question: "When should I book my Dolomites trip?" The honest answer is there's a real trade-off between weather, crowds, and road conditions, and the right answer depends on what you're optimizing for. Here's exactly how I'd think it through if it were my own holiday.

The Short Answer

Mid-June to mid-September is your riding window for the high passes. Outside of that, the highest roads are often still closed or only recently reopened with debris and gravel washed onto the tarmac from winter runoff. Within that window, early-to-mid June and September are the sweet spot for most riders — you get stable weather without peak-summer crowds or heat.

Why the Dolomites Have Such a Short Season

Unlike lower-altitude destinations, several of the region's signature passes — Passo Giau, Passo Fedaia, Passo Pordoi — sit above 2,000m, and some stay snow-affected well into late May in a heavy winter. Local authorities generally clear and reopen roads in stages through May and early June, but exact dates shift year to year depending on snowfall, so it's always worth checking current conditions if you're booking right at the edges of the season.

Month by Month

Late May — Technically possible on lower routes, but risky for a Dolomites-specific trip since higher passes may still be closed or only partially cleared. Not recommended unless your itinerary has flexibility built in.

June — Passes reopen (some as late as the first week of June depending on snowfall), days are long, and temperatures are pleasant rather than punishing. Occasional afternoon storms build through the month, so plan to start rides early. This is my personal favorite month to guide in the Dolomites — the light is incredible, wildflowers are out on the high meadows, and the roads are noticeably quieter than July and August.

July — Warm, settled, and increasingly busy. Italian and German school holidays begin adding domestic tourist traffic to the passes, particularly around the Sella Ronda loop. Still very rideable, just book accommodation early.

August — Peak season, in every sense. This is when Italy itself goes on holiday, and popular passes like Passo Pordoi and Passo Sella get heavy motorbike and car traffic, along with the busiest café stops. Weather is generally the most reliable of the year, but if you can only travel in August, ride the classic climbs early morning before 9am for a noticeably different experience.

September — My other favorite window, and the one I'd recommend to most first-time visitors. Traffic drops off noticeably after the last week of August as domestic tourists head home, temperatures are still very rideable, and the light turns a genuinely golden color on the pale limestone peaks in a way photos never quite capture. There's a slightly higher chance of an early cold snap at altitude by late September, so pack accordingly.

October — Possible on lower valley routes, but higher passes may close without warning if snow arrives early in the month. I wouldn't recommend booking a Dolomites-specific climbing trip this late unless your itinerary is flexible enough to shift to lower-altitude routes if needed.

What About Altitude and Temperature?

The Dolomites climbs regularly take you from valley floors around 1,000–1,400m up to passes at 2,000–2,240m — Passo Giau tops out at 2,236m, Passo Pordoi at 2,239m, Passo Fedaia at 2,057m. That means even in July, a valley morning starting at a comfortable 22°C can turn into a summit arrival at 10°C with wind chill making it feel colder still. Always carry a packable gilet or light jacket, even on a hot day — I've never once regretted bringing one, and I've regretted not having one more than once, usually somewhere windy near a summit café.

Booking Timing and Accommodation

If you want June or September dates, book well in advance — those are the two windows every experienced Dolomites cyclist is trying to get, and good accommodation in towns like Corvara, Cortina d'Ampezzo, Canazei and Arabba fills up fast for those shoulder-season weeks specifically because word has gotten around about how good the conditions are.

A Note on Rest Days and Weather Contingency

Even in the best months, mountain weather in this region can turn quickly. A good itinerary builds in either a flexible day or a lower-altitude backup route, so a single stormy morning doesn't derail an entire trip. This is one of the quieter advantages of a guided tour — local knowledge of which valley roads make a good alternative when the high passes aren't cooperating.

The Short Answer

Mid-June to mid-September is your riding window for the high passes. title.raw: Cycling the Strade Bianche White Roads (Tuscany)
title.rendered: Cycling the Strade Bianche White Roads (Tuscany)

content.raw:
Every March, thousands of cyclists travel to Siena to ride one of the world's most iconic cycling events: the Strade Bianche Gran Fondo.

Following many of the same white roads used by the professional race, the event combines smooth Tuscan tarmac, historic villages and the famous strade bianche — the white limestone roads that have become one of the symbols of Italian cycling.

Whether you are planning to ride the Gran Fondo or simply want to experience these legendary roads yourself, this guide covers everything you need to know.

What are the Strade Bianche?

The strade bianche are centuries-old limestone farm roads that connect vineyards, olive groves and medieval villages throughout the Tuscan countryside around Siena.

Unlike rough gravel trails, these roads are generally compact, smooth and perfectly rideable on a modern road bike. Their unique white surface, rolling terrain and incredible scenery make them one of the most beautiful cycling experiences in Europe.

The roads became internationally famous thanks to the professional Strade Bianche race, first held in 2007 and now considered one of the most prestigious one-day races on the cycling calendar.

Can You Ride Strade Bianche on a Road Bike?

Absolutely.

The Strade Bianche Gran Fondo is designed for road cyclists, and the majority of riders complete it on modern road bikes.

The white roads are fast and compact, but the surface can vary depending on weather conditions. A few simple adjustments will make your experience much more enjoyable:

  • 30-32mm tyres are ideal
  • Tubeless tyres are highly recommended
  • Slightly lower tyre pressures improve comfort and grip
  • Compact gearing helps on the steep Tuscan climbs

A gravel bike can also work well, but it is not necessary unless you plan to explore rougher unpaved roads beyond the classic Strade Bianche sectors.

The Strade Bianche Gran Fondo

Held every March in Siena, the Gran Fondo gives amateur cyclists the opportunity to experience many of the same iconic roads used by the professional race.

The event offers:

  • Start and finish in the historic city of Siena
  • Famous white road sectors from the professional race
  • Thousands of cyclists from around the world
  • The incredible atmosphere of race weekend in Tuscany

It is one of Italy's most unique cycling events and a must-do experience for any passionate cyclist.

Is the Strade Bianche Gran Fondo Difficult?

Despite not featuring long Alpine climbs, the Strade Bianche is a challenging event.

The difficulty comes from the combination of:

  • Constant rolling terrain
  • Short and steep climbs
  • Repeated changes between tarmac and white roads
  • Limited opportunities to recover

Tuscany may look gentle on the map, but the accumulated elevation and constant rhythm changes make this a demanding and rewarding challenge.

Best Time to Ride the Strade Bianche

March is the perfect month if you want to experience the Gran Fondo and the incredible atmosphere surrounding the event.

For riders looking for quieter roads, spring and autumn are also fantastic times to explore Tuscany.

The landscape changes throughout the year:

Summer can be very hot, especially in the exposed Tuscan countryside

Spring brings green hills and wildflowers

Autumn offers vineyards full of colour and harvest season

Bike Setup for the Strade Bianche

For the best experience, we recommend:

Bike

  • Modern road bike
  • 30-32mm tyres where possible
  • Tubeless setup preferred

Equipment

  • Two bottles, as some sections are exposed
  • Lightweight jacket or vest for cooler mornings
  • Sunglasses to protect your eyes from dust and small stones

The key is finding the balance between speed on the tarmac and comfort on the white roads.

Join Our Strade Bianche Cycling Tour

At Cigala Cycling Tours, we organise guided experiences that allow riders to discover the legendary white roads of Tuscany with expert local knowledge, professional support and carefully planned routes.

Whether your goal is to ride the Strade Bianche Gran Fondo, explore the famous race sectors or simply experience Tuscany by bike, we create an unforgettable cycling experience.

Discover our Strade Bianche Cycling Tour

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a gravel bike for Strade Bianche?

No. A modern road bike with wider tyres (around 30-32mm) is perfect for riding the classic Strade Bianche sectors and the Gran Fondo.

Is the Strade Bianche Gran Fondo the same route as the professional race?

The route changes slightly each year, but the Gran Fondo includes many of the iconic white road sectors used by the professional race.

Can beginners ride Strade Bianche?

Yes, but good preparation is recommended. The combination of distance, elevation and changing surfaces makes it a challenging event. There is also the option of the Medio Fondo instead of the Gran Fondo. The Medio Fondo is 80km with approx 1000 mt of elevation.

What tyres are best for Strade Bianche?

For most riders, 30-32mm tubeless road tyres provide the best balance between speed, comfort and confidence.

Should I train specifically for the Strade Bianche Gran Fondo?

Absolutely. While many cyclists can complete the event without following a structured training plan, arriving well prepared will make the experience far more enjoyable.

The repeated climbs, rolling terrain and changing road surfaces make the Strade Bianche more demanding than many riders expect. A personalised training plan can help you improve your climbing, endurance and confidence before race day.

If you'd like expert guidance, explore my personalised cycling coaching at coaching.cigalacycling.com

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours

title.raw: The Col du Galibier: A Cyclist's Guide
title.rendered: The Col du Galibier: A Cyclist’s Guide

content.raw:
The Galibier is one of the great Tour de France mountains, and unlike some famous climbs that disappoint in person once you're actually grinding up them, this one genuinely delivers — long, wild, and increasingly bare of trees the higher you go, until you're riding through what feels like another planet near the summit, all exposed rock and thin alpine air.

A Brief History

The Galibier has featured in the Tour de France more than any other high mountain pass, first climbed by the race in 1911 and included dozens of times since. Henri Desgrange, the race's founder, considered it one of the defining tests of the entire event, and a monument to him stands near the summit tunnel. Riding past it yourself, with the same views the earliest Tour riders would have seen (minus the modern road surface, thankfully), is a genuinely special moment for anyone who follows the sport's history.

Key Numbers

  • Summit elevation: 2,642m
  • From Col du Télégraphe/Valloire side: roughly 18km at an average of 6.9%, with the final few kilometres pushing past 10%
  • Full combined climb (Télégraphe + Galibier from Saint-Michel-de-Maurienne): over 35km of near-continuous climbing, one of the longest sustained ascents in the Alps
  • Tunnel option: a road tunnel near the summit allows you to bypass the very final, steepest ramps if needed, though most cyclists prefer to take the exposed road over the top for the views and the sense of completion

The final stretch above the treeline is where it gets serious — thinner air, exposed rock, and a gradient that steepens right when your legs least want it to, with switchbacks that expose you fully to whatever wind is coming off the surrounding peaks.

Which Direction to Climb

Most riders take it from Valloire, having already warmed up over the Col du Télégraphe on the way. This combination is the classic Tour de France approach and gives you a natural rhythm — a warm-up climb through forest, a short, fast descent into Valloire, then the main event starting fresh from the valley floor.

Climbing from the other direction, via the Col du Lautaret, is shorter but arrives at a steeper average gradient with less of a natural rhythm-building warm-up — a legitimate option if your itinerary approaches from that side, but generally considered the harder of the two main approaches for a first attempt.

Weather Warning

This is a genuinely high alpine pass, and conditions change fast, even by Alpine standards. Even in July, it's common to find the summit 15–20°C colder than the valley, with wind that can be genuinely brutal and cut straight through a thin jersey. Snow is possible even in midsummer in a bad year — I've personally ridden through light snowfall at the summit in early July. Always carry a proper packable jacket, not just a gilet, for this climb specifically; it's one of the few places in the Alps where I'd say a gilet alone genuinely isn't enough.

Tips From the Road

Pace the lower slopes conservatively — riders who go hard through the forested lower section, where the gradient feels deceptively manageable, almost always pay for it above the treeline, where there's no shade, no let-up, and the psychological weight of visible switchbacks stacking up ahead of you. Settle into a rhythm you could hold for two hours, not twenty minutes, and resist the temptation to chase other riders on the lower slopes.

Fuel properly before the final push — the last few kilometres above the treeline are where most riders' pace drops off, and having enough in the tank for that section matters more than a fast start.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

The Galibier is one of the centerpiece climbs on our French Alps cycling tour, ridden as part of a week built around the same roads the Tour de France uses almost every year. Full support vehicle backup means you can push yourself on the climb without worrying about the logistics of a mechanical issue or needing a lift on a tough day — the van is always within reach.

If you'd like to tackle the Galibier from a different base, combine it with other French Alps climbs, or build a longer trip around this region, we're also happy to design a fully custom tour for your group.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Col du Galibier harder than the Col du Tourmalet?
They're comparable in overall difficulty, though the Galibier's exposed upper section and thinner air at higher elevation make the final kilometres feel notably harder than the Tourmalet's steepest ramps.

Can I skip the very top section using the tunnel?
Yes, a road tunnel bypasses the final steep ramps near the true summit — some riders use this on a tough day, though most prefer completing the full climb for the views and sense of achievement.

What's the best month to attempt the Galibier?
July and August offer the most reliable road conditions and weather, though the pass typically isn't fully clear of snow debris until mid-to-late June, and afternoon storms are a real risk in high summer, so early starts are essential.

Do I need special gearing for this climb?
A compact chainset with an easy enough cassette to spin rather than grind the steeper upper sections is strongly recommended — this isn't a climb to attempt on a straight 53/39 setup unless you're an exceptionally strong climber.

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours

title.rendered: Cycling in the Pyrenees: Best Climbs

content.raw:
The Pyrenees don't get quite the same spotlight as the Alps, and honestly, that works in your favor — quieter roads, fewer tour buses, and climbs that are every bit as demanding as their more famous Alpine cousins. Here's how I'd match a route to your level, based on years of guiding riders across the full range of experience through this region.

Why the Pyrenees Feel Different From the Alps

The roads here tend to be narrower and quieter than their Alpine counterparts, with a wilder, more rural character — you're as likely to be held up by a flock of grazing sheep crossing the road as by traffic. The mountains themselves are geologically older and, in places, feel more raw and less manicured for tourism, which a lot of experienced cyclists actually prefer. title.raw: What to Pack for a European Cycling Holiday
title.rendered: What to Pack for a European Cycling Holiday

content.raw:
After a decade of guiding trips across Europe, I've seen every packing mistake there is — overpacked kit bags, forgotten gilets, saddles that didn't survive the flight. So here's the list I actually give my own clients before they travel, organized by what genuinely matters versus what's optional.

On-Bike Essentials

A helmet you already trust — most rental setups include helmets, but if you have strong preferences on fit, bringing your own removes one variable.

2–3 kits (jersey + shorts) — you'll ride most days, and hotel laundry isn't always reliable or same-day, especially in smaller towns. Two to three sets, rotated and hand-washed if needed, is genuinely enough for a week.

A packable rain jacket — even in the Mediterranean, mountain weather turns fast, and every destination we operate in has at least some route sections at meaningful altitude where conditions can shift within an hour.

Arm/leg warmers — mornings are colder than you expect, especially at altitude or in shoulder-season months, and warmers pack down small enough that there's no real downside to bringing them even if you don't end up needing them every day.

A gilet for descents — this is the single most under-packed item I see, and the one riders most often wish they'd brought after a cold descent leaves them shivering at the bottom of a climb.

Your own saddle (if riding a rental bike) — comfort is deeply personal, and this is the one component worth the minor hassle of packing and transferring, since an unfamiliar saddle is one of the fastest ways to turn a great week into an uncomfortable one.

Cycling sunglasses with interchangeable lenses for variable light, particularly useful moving between bright coastal roads and shaded mountain forest sections on the same day.

Off-Bike

  • Comfortable walking shoes for evenings exploring towns — cycling shoes are not made for cobblestones, and most of our destinations have genuinely walkable historic centers worth exploring after a ride.
  • A layer for cool evenings, even in summer, since mountain and coastal towns alike often cool down noticeably after sunset.
  • A small day bag for anything you want on non-riding excursions or rest days.
  • A swimsuit if your itinerary includes any lake or coastal destinations — Lake Garda, Lake Como, Croatia, and the Algarve all offer excellent post-ride swimming.

What NOT to Overpack

Most riders bring too many kits and not enough warm layers. Two to three sets of riding kit is genuinely enough for a week-long guided tour — you're not racing, you're touring, and hotel sinks exist. Similarly, riders often bring far more casual clothing than they end up wearing, since most evenings on a cycling tour are fairly low-key after a full day on the bike.

Travel Logistics

A charging cable/adapter appropriate to your destination country — obvious, but the most commonly forgotten item on any trip

Check your airline's bike/luggage policy well in advance if bringing your own bike, since policies and fees vary significantly between carriers and can change seasonally

A basic multi-tool and spare tube, even on guided tours with mechanical support, for the rare moment you need something before the support van arrives

A phone mount if you like to follow routes yourself, though guided groups generally won't strictly need this since you're following the guide directly

Travel insurance that covers cycling activities specifically — worth double-checking, since some general travel policies exclude cycling or treat it as an "adventure sport" requiring additional coverage

Bike Transport: Bringing Your Own vs. Renting

If you're bringing your own bike, a hard case offers the best protection but is bulkier to transport to and from airports; a padded soft case is lighter and easier to manage but offers less protection against rough handling. Either way, remove the pedals, deflate tyres slightly, and protect the rear derailleur specifically, since it's the most commonly damaged component in transit.

If you'd rather avoid the hassle entirely, premium road and gravel rental bikes are available on every one of our tours, professionally sized and set up before you arrive — worth strongly considering if your own bike travel logistics feel like more stress than they're worth.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

Every one of our guided cycling tours includes a full kit list specific to that trip's terrain and season, sent well ahead of departure — so you're never guessing what a particular climate or route actually demands, and you arrive with exactly what you need rather than either an overstuffed bag or a missing essential.

If your trip has specific needs beyond a standard departure, we're also happy to design a fully custom tour and tailor the kit guidance to match.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need to bring my own bike, or is rental good enough?
Rental bikes on our tours are premium, well-maintained road or gravel bikes, professionally fitted on arrival — entirely sufficient for the vast majority of guests. Bringing your own is mainly worth it if you have specific fit or component preferences.

What's the single most forgotten item you see?
A packable rain jacket or gilet, hands down. Riders consistently underestimate how much temperature and weather can shift at altitude, even on a forecasted sunny day.

Should I bring cycling shoes with road cleats, or is it destination-dependent?
This depends on whether your tour is road or gravel-focused — check your specific tour's bike style before packing, since gravel tours may use a different cleat/pedal system than pure road tours.

How should I protect my bike if flying with my own?
A hard case is the safest option for checked bike transport, though a well-padded soft case is a reasonable compromise if you're managing your own transport to and from airports without assistance.

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours

title.raw: Gravel Cycling in Cyprus: Where to Ride
title.rendered: Gravel Cycling in Cyprus: Where to Ride

content.raw:
Cyprus doesn't come up often in cycling conversations, which is exactly why I love guiding here — you get Mediterranean roads and genuine mountain terrain, almost entirely to yourself, in a climate that works for riding nearly year-round in a way few other European destinations can match.

Why Cyprus Works So Well for Winter Cycling

While most of Europe's classic cycling regions shut down for winter, Cyprus's position at the eastern edge of the Mediterranean gives it a genuinely mild climate through the cooler months — this is part of why it's become a quiet favorite among professional teams for early-season training camps, alongside the more famous Mallorca and Tenerife options.

The Troodos Mountains

This is the heart of Cyprus cycling — a range of forested climbs reaching over 1,900m at Mount Olympus (the island's highest point, not to be confused with the more famous Greek mountain of the same name), with a mix of quiet paved roads and well-maintained gravel forestry tracks winding through Aleppo pine and cedar forest. Gradients are moderate but sustained, and the pine forest cover makes for a welcome break from the more exposed, sun-baked coastal roads.

The forestry tracks around Troodos are genuinely excellent gravel riding — wide enough to feel safe and predictable, well-drained thanks to the mountain's rocky base, and largely free of the technical obstacles you'd find on true singletrack. This is approachable gravel riding for anyone comfortable on a road bike, not a mountain-biking test.

Coastal Roads

The southern coast around Limassol and Paphos offers flatter, faster riding with sea views most of the way — a good complement to the mountain days, and ideal for an easier recovery ride between harder Troodos outings. The Akamas Peninsula in the west offers a wilder, less developed coastal option for those wanting a quieter alternative to the more built-up southern coast.

Best Time to Ride

October through April is the sweet spot. Cyprus is genuinely one of the best winter cycling destinations in Europe — daytime temperatures typically sit in the mid-teens to low 20s°C even in January, while northern Europe is under snow and most Alpine and Pyrenean roads are closed entirely. Summer (June–August) is better avoided for serious climbing days; the heat in the lowlands is intense, regularly exceeding 35°C, though the higher elevation of Troodos does offer some relief even in midsummer.

Bike Choice

A gravel bike with 35mm+ tyres opens up the forestry tracks in Troodos that a road bike simply can't access comfortably, while still being entirely comfortable on the coastal tarmac sections. If your trip is coastal-only, a standard road bike is perfectly fine, but you'd be missing what makes Cyprus genuinely distinctive as a cycling destination.

What to Pack

Layering matters more in Cyprus than the "sunny Mediterranean island" reputation suggests — Troodos at 1,900m in winter can be noticeably cold, occasionally with light snow at the very highest points, while the coast the same day might be a mild 18°C. A packable layer for the mountain days, alongside standard warm-weather kit for the coast, covers the full range you'll encounter.

Common Mistakes First-Timers Make

Underestimating the Troodos climbs is the most common one — because Cyprus has a reputation as a beach destination, riders sometimes arrive expecting flat, easy riding and are surprised by the genuine mountain terrain in the interior. Treat the Troodos days with the same respect you'd give an Alpine climbing day.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

Our Cyprus Crossing Gravel tour combines the rugged climbs of the Troodos Mountains with spectacular Mediterranean coastal riding, perfectly timed for spring when Cyprus offers some of the best cycling conditions in Europe. It's become one of our most popular early-season trips, giving riders the chance to enjoy warm sunshine, epic mountain roads, and stunning coastlines while much of Europe is still in the grip of winter.

If you'd like a different balance of mountain versus coastal riding, or want a trip timed specifically around a winter training block, we're also happy to design a fully custom tour around Cyprus for your group.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Cyprus a good destination for a winter training camp?
Yes — this is exactly why professional teams have used it, alongside Mallorca and Tenerife, as an early-season base. Mild temperatures and genuine climbing terrain make it well suited to structured winter training.

Do I need a gravel bike, or is a road bike enough?
A road bike handles the coastal riding well, but a gravel bike is recommended to access the full range of Troodos and enjoy a full gravel tour with forestry tracks, which are a highlight of the region.

How does the climbing in Troodos compare to the Alps or Pyrenees?
Shorter and generally less steep than the Alps' signature passes, but genuinely substantial climbing nonetheless, particularly cumulative elevation gain over a full riding day.

Is Cyprus cycling suitable for beginners?
The coastal routes suit a wide range of fitness levels well; the Troodos mountain days are better suited to riders with at least moderate climbing experience.

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours

title.raw: Road vs. Gravel Bike: Which Should You Bring?
title.rendered: Road vs. Gravel Bike: Which Should You Bring?

content.raw:
This is one of the first questions I get from anyone booking a trip, and the honest answer is: it depends entirely on the destination, not on which bike you personally prefer riding at home. Here's a genuinely practical breakdown to help you decide, rather than a generic "it depends" that leaves you no better off.

The Core Difference That Actually Matters

Beyond tyre width, the real distinction between a road and gravel setup for touring purposes comes down to what surfaces you'll actually encounter. Destinations built around paved mountain passes and coastal roads — the Dolomites, French Alps, Pyrenees, Lake Garda, Lake Como, the Algarve, Croatia's coastal routes — are almost entirely tarmac. title.rendered: How to Prepare for a Cycling Holiday

content.raw:
You don't need to arrive in race shape for a guided cycling holiday, but a little structured preparation makes the difference between surviving a big mountain week and actually enjoying it. Here's the simple timeline I give my own coaching clients, built around the same principles I use training for my own racing season, just scaled appropriately for a touring holiday rather than competition.

12 Weeks Out: Build a Base

Focus on consistent, easy-to-moderate rides 3-4 times a week. The goal here isn't intensity — it's time in the saddle, so your body gets used to riding on consecutive days, which is very different physiologically from a single weekend ride, however long that single ride might be. Aim for a mix of ride lengths, with at least one longer ride each week that gradually extends over this period.

If you're newer to structured training, this is also the phase to establish a consistent bike position and confirm your setup is comfortable for extended periods — discomfort issues that seem minor on a 45-minute ride become genuinely problematic on a multi-hour touring day.

8 Weeks Out: Add Some Climbing

If you have any hills near you, start including them weekly, ideally with some repeated efforts on the same climb to track improvement over the following weeks. If you don't have access to hills, longer steady efforts on the flat (20-40 minutes at a sustainable, slightly uncomfortable pace — roughly what you could hold in conversation but not comfortably) build similar aerobic fitness, even without the specific climbing-muscle adaptation.

This is also the point to start riding back-to-back days on weekends if your schedule allows — mimicking the physical demand of a multi-day tour, where fatigue compounds across consecutive days rather than resetting overnight the way a single hard ride followed by rest days does.

6 Weeks Out: Introduce Some Intensity

A weekly session with sustained harder efforts — intervals of 8-15 minutes at a genuinely uncomfortable but sustainable pace — builds the kind of fitness that makes climbs feel more manageable without requiring race-specific training. This doesn't need to be complicated; even simply picking a local hill and riding it hard once a week provides most of the benefit.

4 Weeks Out: Simulate the Trip

Try to string together 2-3 consecutive riding days, even if shorter in distance than your actual tour days. This tells you far more about your readiness than any single long ride will, since tour fatigue is cumulative rather than about any one day's distance or elevation. Pay attention to how your legs feel on day two and three specifically — that's the fitness quality your actual holiday will demand most.

2 Weeks Out: Taper

Reduce volume noticeably, but keep some intensity in shorter efforts, and prioritize sleep over squeezing in extra rides. This is where many riders go wrong — they cram extra training right before departure, arriving tired rather than fresh, which undoes much of the benefit of the previous weeks' consistent work. Trust the base you've built; a tapered, rested rider consistently outperforms an overtrained, fatigued one on tour, regardless of raw fitness numbers.

What Actually Matters Most

Time in the saddle beats raw power for a touring holiday. If you can comfortably ride 60-90 minutes several days in a row without significant discomfort or excessive fatigue, you have the base fitness for the vast majority of our tours — the guided pace, rest stops, and support vehicle backup do a lot of the rest, and you're not being asked to sustain race-pace efforts for hours at a time.

Nutrition and Hydration Habits Worth Building Beforehand

Practicing your on-bike fueling strategy during training rides, rather than figuring it out for the first time on tour, makes a genuine difference. If you're not used to eating regularly during longer rides, start building that habit now — a multi-day tour with cumulative fatigue is exactly the wrong time to discover you don't fuel well on the bike.

Common Preparation Mistakes

The most common mistake is treating preparation as purely about fitness volume and ignoring bike-specific conditioning — a rider who runs or does other cardio regularly but rarely cycles will still find cycling-specific muscles fatigue faster than their general fitness level would suggest. Time on an actual bike, even if shorter than your target, beats equivalent time on other cardio equipment.

The second common mistake is over-preparing on the final week rather than resting — see the taper note above.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

Every trip lists an expected daily distance and elevation profile so you can prepare specifically — check the details on your chosen tour page, and feel free to reach out if you want a tailored prep plan; this is exactly the kind of thing our coaching side handles, with structured plans built around your specific tour's demands and your current fitness level.

If you'd like an itinerary built specifically around your group's fitness level and timeline, we're also happy to design a fully custom tour.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many weeks of preparation do I really need for a moderate tour like Croatia or the Algarve?
Even 6-8 weeks of consistent riding 3 times a week makes a meaningful difference for these less climbing-intensive destinations, though the general timeline above still applies proportionally.

Do I need a coach to prepare properly, or can I follow a general plan?A general training plan like the one above is more than enough for most recreational cyclists looking to enjoy the trip and complete the rides comfortably. However, if you're preparing for a more demanding challenge—such as the Dolomites, Stelvio, or the Pyrenees—or you're limited by time and want to maximise every training session, personalised coaching can make a significant difference.

At Cigala Cycling Coaching, I create individual training plans based on your current fitness, goals, available training time, and the demands of your chosen event or cycling holiday. Whether you're aiming to simply reach the finish or perform at your very best, a tailored approach helps you arrive stronger, more confident, and ready to enjoy every kilometre.

Interested in personalised coaching? Explore my coaching programmes or get in touch to discuss the best option for your goals.

What if I can't manage consecutive training days due to my schedule?
Focus instead on extending your longest single ride each week and don't worry excessively about the consecutive-day simulation — it's valuable but not essential, and guided tours with support vehicles are more forgiving of this gap than an unsupported multi-day ride would be.

Is strength training worth adding alongside cycling-specific preparation?
Yes, particularly for climbing-focused destinations — general lower body and core strength work complements cycling-specific fitness well and can help with sustained climbing efforts.

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours

content.raw:
One of the most common messages I get before someone books is some version of "am I fit enough for this?" So here's a straightforward way to think about it, without the guesswork, built from years of matching riders of every level to the right trip.

Why This Question Matters More Than People Realize

A mismatched fitness level is, in my experience, the single biggest thing that can spoil an otherwise well-run trip. Not because anyone gets left behind — our support structure prevents that — but because a rider who's constantly at their absolute limit doesn't get to enjoy the scenery, the food, or the camaraderie of a group tour the way someone riding within their capability does. Getting this right upfront matters more than most people assume when booking.

Leisure / Moderate Fitness

If you ride a few times a month, can comfortably manage 40-60km with some rolling hills, and aren't looking to push your limits on holiday, the Algarve and Croatia coastal tours are excellent fits. Rolling terrain, stunning scenery, and daily distances that leave plenty of energy for the food and culture side of the trip rather than leaving you depleted by dinner.

These tours suit riders who cycle recreationally, perhaps commute occasionally, or simply want an active holiday without the specific demands of high-mountain climbing.

Solid Recreational Rider

If you ride regularly, are comfortable with 60-90km days and can handle sustained climbs without needing to walk any section, Lake Garda, Lake Como, and Tuscany are well suited — real climbing, but with enough variety in daily profile that no single day is overwhelming, and rest days or shorter options built into the itinerary.

This category covers the majority of our guests — people who ride consistently, perhaps do the occasional organized sportive or gran fondo at home, and want a genuine challenge without needing to be at peak competitive fitness.

Strong, Experienced Climber

If you actively train for climbing, ride 100km+ days at home, and want to genuinely test yourself against legendary gradients, the Dolomites, French Alps, and Pyrenees tours are built for you — these are the tours where the climbs are the main event, not a side feature, and the itinerary is structured around tackling genuinely demanding Tour de France and Giro d'Italia climbs.

What About Gravel-Specific Fitness Demands?

Our Cyprus and Tuscany gravel tours have a slightly different fitness profile — the terrain itself is less about pure climbing gradient and more about sustained effort over rolling, mixed-surface terrain. A rider with solid general endurance but less specific mountain-climbing experience often finds these tours a great fit.

A Few Honest Notes

  • Every tour includes a support vehicle, so no one is ever left to struggle alone on a climb — that safety net exists regardless of fitness level, and it fundamentally changes the risk calculation compared to an unsupported ride
  • Groups are small and paced flexibly, so a mixed-ability group can genuinely still ride together for most of a route, splitting only where the terrain specifically calls for it
  • If you're between categories, it's always worth messaging us directly — matching people to the right trip properly is something we take seriously, since getting this right is one of the biggest factors in whether a guest has a great week or a merely good one

How Age Factors Into This (Or Doesn't)

I want to be clear that this framework is about current fitness and riding habits, not age. We've guided guests well into their 70s on our harder mountain tours, and equally, some younger riders find our "moderate" tours plenty challenging if they're newer to consistent cycling. Recent, consistent riding habit matters far more than age as a predictor of how a guest will handle a given tour.

How We Can Help You Decide

If you're still unsure, tell us your typical weekly riding volume, your longest recent ride, and how comfortable you are on sustained climbs, and we'll point you to the right tour — it takes two minutes and saves a lot of second-guessing, both before booking and on the road itself.

Frequently Asked Questions

What if my fitness doesn't clearly fit one category?
Most riders sit somewhere between categories, which is completely normal — message us with specifics and we'll recommend the best fit, sometimes suggesting a tour one level below what you might initially assume so you genuinely enjoy the week rather than just surviving it.

Can I upgrade my fitness closer to departure if I'm borderline for a harder tour?
Yes, and our preparation guide outlines a structured approach — a borderline rider who commits to consistent training in the 8-12 weeks before departure can genuinely move up a category.

Do harder tours require you to keep pace with a fast group?
No — group pace is set to be inclusive, and support vehicle backup means slower riders are never left stranded, though the terrain itself on our hardest tours is objectively more demanding regardless of pace.

Is it possible to do a custom trip that mixes difficulty levels for a group with mixed fitness?
Yes, this is one of the more common requests for our custom tours, and we regularly design itineraries that let a mixed-ability group travel together while offering optional harder or easier routes on specific days.

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours
