title.raw: Why Lake Garda Is Italy's Best-Kept Cycling Secret
title.rendered: Why Lake Garda Is Italy’s Best-Kept Cycling Secret

content.raw:
Ask most people to name Italy's great cycling regions and you'll hear the Dolomites, maybe Tuscany. Lake Garda rarely comes up first, which is strange, because it's genuinely one of the best all-around cycling destinations in the country, and it's exactly why professional teams have quietly used it as a training base for decades, long before it became a wider cycling-tourism destination.

A Region Built Around Water and Mountains at Once

What makes Garda unusual among Italian cycling destinations is the collision of two very different landscapes within a short ride of each other. To the south, the lake basin opens into gentle, almost Mediterranean terrain — olive groves, lemon houses, flat lakeside promenades. Head north along either shore, though, and the terrain changes fast, with the lake narrowing between steep limestone cliffs as you approach the foothills of the Alps proper. Few destinations let you ride both characters of landscape in the same week, let alone the same day.

Diverse Riding, All in One Place

Garda's real advantage is variety within a small radius. You can ride flat, fast lakeside roads through olive groves one day, tackle rolling hills around Valpolicella wine country the next — home to the grapes behind Amarone and Valpolicella wines — and then head north for genuine mountain climbing toward the Alps, all without changing hotels or facing long transfer days between riding regions.

The western shore, through towns like Salò and Gargnano, offers some of the most scenic lakeside riding in the country, with the road cut directly into cliffside in places, tunnels included, right at the water's edge. The eastern shore around Malcesine and Torbole trades some of that drama for wider roads and easier access to the northern mountain routes.

The Optional Stelvio Day

This is the region's trump card. On our September departure, a day trip from Lake Garda gets you to the base of the Passo dello Stelvio, Italy's highest paved pass and one of the most famous climbs in the sport, covered in detail in our Stelvio Pass guide. Very few lake-based destinations put a climb of that caliber within reach of a single day excursion, and having that option available on this specific departure, alongside gentler lakeside days either side of it, gives our September Garda trip a rare structural advantage.

Climate

Lake Garda has a genuinely mild microclimate — the surrounding mountains and the lake's thermal mass create conditions closer to the Mediterranean than you'd expect this far north and this close to the Alps, a phenomenon locals will tell you has shaped agriculture here for centuries, allowing olives and even lemons to grow at a latitude where they otherwise wouldn't survive winter. This microclimate means a longer riding season than most Alpine regions and comfortable temperatures well into spring and autumn, often extending the practical riding season by several weeks compared to purely Alpine destinations.

The Ora Wind

Cyclists who've ridden here before will know about the Ora, a reliable thermal wind that builds through the morning and blows north up the lake most afternoons in the warmer months. It's predictable enough that experienced local riders and windsurfers alike plan around it, and it can turn what feels like an easy tailwind-assisted morning into a genuinely challenging headwind return leg if you're not paying attention to timing.

Food and Culture

The region blends Lombardy, Veneto, and Trentino-Alto Adige culinary traditions depending on which shore you're on, plus some of Italy's best lakeside towns for an evening walk after a big ride — Sirmione's historic old town on its narrow peninsula, Malcesine's castle overlooking the water, and Riva del Garda's mountain-backed setting at the lake's northern tip all reward the effort of getting there on two wheels rather than by car or ferry.

Common Mistakes First-Timers Make

The most common mistake is underestimating how different the northern and southern parts of the lake feel, and planning a single "lake loop" without accounting for the genuine mountain terrain to the north. The second is not accounting for the Ora wind when planning ride timing — a morning start heading north with the wind, returning south into a building headwind in the afternoon, is a very different day than the reverse.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

Our Lake Garda cycling tour is built around exactly this variety — lakeside days, hill country, and, on our September departure specifically, the option to summit the Stelvio as a day trip. It's one of our most requested trips, and once people ride it, I understand why it becomes an annual habit for a lot of our returning guests.

If the standard itinerary doesn't quite match what you're after, whether that's more time in Valpolicella wine country, a longer or shorter Stelvio option, or combining Garda with another nearby region, we can also design a fully custom tour built around this area specifically for your group.ht tour — it takes two minutes and saves a lot of second-guessing, both before booking and on the road itself.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Lake Garda a good destination for a mixed-ability group?
Yes, more so than most single-character destinations — the southern lakeside routes suit less experienced riders well, while the northern routes and optional Stelvio day give stronger riders a genuine challenge, all within the same trip.

How long is a day trip to the Stelvio from a Lake Garda base?
It's a full riding day with a support vehicle transfer to the base of the climb, generally making for one of the longer, more demanding days of a Garda-based week. Note this option currently runs on our September departure specifically — if you're booking a different date and want the Stelvio included, our Italian Alps trip covers it as part of the core itinerary.

What's the best base town for a Lake Garda cycling trip?
This depends on your priorities — Riva del Garda suits those wanting quick access to northern mountain routes, while a more central or southern base suits riders prioritizing the gentler lakeside and Valpolicella riding.

Can Lake Garda be combined with other nearby regions on a custom trip?
Yes, its position makes it a natural base to combine with Lake Como or parts of the Dolomites on an extended custom itinerary, which is one of the more popular custom trip requests we receive for this region.

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours

title.raw: Cycling Croatia's Adriatic Coast: A First-Timer's Guide
title.rendered: Cycling Croatia’s Adriatic Coast: A First-Timer’s Guide

content.raw:
Croatia has quietly become one of my favorite places to guide — a stunning, underrated coastline, genuinely good road surfaces, and an island-hopping element that most European cycling destinations simply don't offer. This guide covers everything I'd want a first-timer to know before booking.

Why Croatia Stands Apart From Other Coastal Cycling Destinations

Most coastal cycling destinations in Europe give you one thing: a coastline. Croatia gives you a coastline plus a genuinely unique archipelago of islands just offshore, connected by a well-run network of car and passenger ferries. That combination — riding a stretch of mainland coast, then boarding a short ferry to continue the ride on an island, then perhaps another ferry to a second island before returning to the mainland — creates a rhythm and variety that a purely linear coastal route can't match.

What the Terrain Is Actually Like

The coastal roads themselves are mostly rolling rather than flat — expect regular short, punchy climbs as the road winds in and out of coves and around limestone headlands, with the sea visible for long stretches at a time. It's rarely flat, but rarely brutally steep either, which makes for genuinely enjoyable, varied riding that suits a broad range of fitness levels better than either a pure mountain destination or a completely flat coastal ride would.

The islands themselves vary in character. Some, like parts of Hvar and Korčula, have their own interior hills worth exploring beyond the coastal ring road, adding a bit of genuine climbing to what might otherwise be a purely coastal itinerary.

The Island Element in Detail

Part of what makes Croatia special is incorporating short ferry crossings between islands and the mainland — a rare chance to combine cycling with a bit of boat travel, seeing the coastline from the water as well as the road, and giving your legs a genuine rest during the crossing itself. It adds a different rhythm to the week compared to a purely point-to-point mainland tour, and the views back toward the coast from a ferry deck are some of the best photo opportunities of the entire trip.

Ferry schedules are generally reliable in the main cycling season (May through September), though it's worth building some flexibility into an itinerary around them rather than planning an extremely tight connection, since even reliable services occasionally run behind schedule.

Road Conditions and Traffic

Main coastal roads can carry more traffic in peak summer, particularly near larger towns and the busiest tourist hubs, so experienced local routing tends to work around the busiest stretches wherever a good quieter alternative exists. Quieter island roads and mainland backroads away from the main coastal highway are where the riding really shines, and where you'll find yourself sharing the road with very little beyond the occasional local moped.

Best Time to Go

May, June, and September are ideal — warm without the intense July/August heat, and noticeably quieter on the roads and in the towns themselves. July and August are beautiful but bring both heat and heavier tourist traffic, especially in well-known towns like Dubrovnik and Split, where cruise ship arrivals can noticeably swell daytime crowds in the old town centers.

October remains rideable and increasingly popular with cyclists specifically seeking the shoulder-season quiet, though some tourist infrastructure (certain restaurants, smaller ferry schedules) begins scaling back for the winter.

Food and Culture Along the Way

Coastal Croatia's cuisine leans heavily Mediterranean with strong Italian influence in places, a legacy of the region's long history under Venetian rule — excellent fresh seafood, good local olive oil, and local wines (particularly from the Pelješac peninsula) that pair well with a week of riding. Stopping in the old stone harbor towns for lunch is as much a part of the experience as the cycling itself, and the historic centers of towns like Rovinj, Trogir, and Korčula town are genuinely worth the extra twenty minutes of wandering after you've locked up the bikes.

What to Pack Specifically for This Trip

Beyond the standard kit covered in our packing guide, a swimsuit is essential here — the combination of coastal riding and clear Adriatic water makes a post-ride swim one of the genuine highlights of the trip, and several of our route stops are chosen specifically with a swimming break in mind.

Common Mistakes First-Timers Make

The most common mistake is underestimating the cumulative climbing on what looks, from a map, like a flat coastal route — the constant small climbs in and out of coves add up over a full day more than the elevation profile might initially suggest. The second is not building in enough buffer time around ferry crossings, particularly in peak season when queues can occasionally run long.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

Our Croatia coastal cycling tour is designed around this exact rhythm — coastal roads, island connections by ferry, and enough variety in daily distance that it suits a broad range of fitness levels, not just strong climbers.

If you'd like a different mix of islands, a longer or shorter itinerary, or want to combine the coastal riding with more inland exploration, we're also happy to design a fully custom tour around this region specifically for your group.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many islands does a typical Croatia cycling tour visit?
This varies by itinerary, but a well-paced week typically includes two to three islands alongside mainland coastal riding, balanced to avoid excessive ferry-hopping that would eat into actual riding time.

Is Croatia suitable for a first-time cycling holiday, or is it better for experienced tourers?
It's genuinely one of the more approachable destinations we offer, with rolling rather than mountainous terrain, making it a good fit for confident recreational riders even without extensive climbing experience.

Do I need to bring anything specific for the ferry crossings?
Just standard travel documents and the swimsuit mentioned above — bikes are easily accommodated on the passenger and car ferries used on our routes.

What's the water temperature like for swimming during the cycling season?
The Adriatic is genuinely swimmable from late May through September, typically reaching comfortable temperatures by June and staying warm into early autumn.

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours

title.raw: The Tuscany Gravel Tour: Riding the Tuscany Trail
title.rendered: The Tuscany Gravel Tour: Riding the Tuscany Trail

content.raw:
If you've read our Strade Bianche guide, you'll know that's focused on the famous white gravel roads around Siena. Our Tuscany Gravel Tour offers a different experience, inspired by the legendary Tuscany Trail and showcasing a much broader cross-section of the region. Instead of concentrating on one area, you'll discover mountains, forests, vineyards, medieval villages, and the wild landscapes of southern Tuscany on a fully supported cycling holiday.

Note: The Tuscany Trail is an independent bikepacking event and route. Cigala Cycling Tours is not affiliated with or endorsed by the Tuscany Trail organisation.

What Is the Tuscany Trail?

The Tuscany Trail is one of Europe's best-known gravel bikepacking routes. Stretching for more than 500 km across Tuscany, it links the northern coast with southern Tuscany using gravel roads, forest tracks, farm lanes, and quiet secondary roads.

Every spring, thousands of cyclists take part in the unsupported Tuscany Trail event, carrying all of their own equipment and completing the route at their own pace. Outside the event, the Tuscany Trail remains one of Italy's most popular long-distance gravel adventures for riders looking to explore Tuscany beyond its famous tourist destinations.

Rather than following a single famous road, the Tuscany Trail connects many of Tuscany's most spectacular landscapes, from the Apuan Alps and Chianti to the Val d'Orcia and the Maremma.

How Our Tuscany Gravel Tour Differs

Our Tuscany Gravel Tour is inspired by some of the finest sections of the Tuscany Trail while following our own carefully designed itinerary.

Instead of tackling the route as an unsupported bikepacking challenge, you'll enjoy:

  • Boutique hotels each night
  • Daily luggage transfers
  • Support vehicle throughout the tour
  • Professional ride leaders
  • Carefully selected stages that maximise the scenery while avoiding unnecessary transfers

The result is a tour that captures the spirit of the Tuscany Trail while allowing you to simply enjoy the riding.

What the Terrain Is Like

One of the reasons the Tuscany Trail has become so popular is the incredible variety of riding.

During the week you'll encounter:

  • Smooth Strade Bianche white gravel roads
  • Rolling vineyard tracks
  • Fast gravel farm roads
  • Forest double-track
  • Quiet tarmac linking remote villages
  • Occasional rougher gravel sections through woodland on the via Francigena

Compared with the classic Strade Bianche sectors around Siena, the terrain is considerably more varied, more gravel, making every day feel different.

Regions You'll Ride Through

The Apuan Alps

The northern mountains of Tuscany offer forest roads, panoramic climbing, and spectacular views towards the famous marble quarries around Carrara.

Chianti

Rolling vineyards, cypress-lined roads, medieval villages, and some of Italy's most famous wine-producing landscapes.

Val d'Orcia

Perhaps Tuscany's most iconic scenery, with endless rolling hills, quiet gravel roads, and UNESCO World Heritage landscapes.

The Maremma

Southern Tuscany has a completely different feel. Wild, rugged, and far quieter than the famous wine regions, it's one of Italy's hidden gems for gravel riding.

Bike Setup

Unlike riding only the Strade Bianche roads, this tour covers a wider range of surfaces.

We recommend:

  • Gravel bike
  • 40–45 mm tyres
  • Low climbing gears
  • Tubeless setup where possible

A modern gravel bike provides the comfort and confidence needed for the more technical forest sections while remaining fast on Tuscany's smoother gravel roads.

Best Time to Ride

Spring (April–May) and autumn (September–October) offer the best cycling conditions.

These months bring:

  • Mild temperatures
  • Green countryside
  • Quiet roads
  • Ideal gravel conditions

Summer can become extremely hot, particularly through the exposed landscapes of southern Tuscany.

Common Mistakes First-Time Riders Make

Many riders assume the Tuscany Trail is simply an extended version of the Strade Bianche roads.

In reality, it's far more varied.

The biggest mistakes include:

  • Bringing tyres that are too narrow
  • Underestimating the climbing
  • Expecting every gravel road to be smooth white limestone
  • Carrying unnecessary equipment

Our guided tour removes these concerns by providing mechanical support, luggage transfers, and experienced local guides throughout the week.

Experience Tuscany Without the Bikepacking Challenge

The unsupported Tuscany Trail is an unforgettable adventure, but it's also a demanding bikepacking event.

Our Tuscany Gravel Tour lets you experience many of the same spectacular landscapes without carrying camping equipment or spending each evening searching for accommodation.

Instead, you'll finish every ride knowing your luggage is already waiting for you, your hotel is booked, and dinner is taken care of—allowing you to focus entirely on enjoying the ride.

If you'd like an itinerary that combines the famous Strade Bianche roads with sections inspired by the Tuscany Trail, we can also create a fully customised private cycling tour tailored to your goals.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

Our Tuscany Epic Gravel Tour is built around these Tuscany Trail highlights, supported and paced very differently from the unsupported bikepacking event it draws from — proper beds, a support van, and a pace that lets you enjoy the Maremma's wild beauty and Chianti's wine country without carrying camping gear on your back.

If you'd like to attempt a longer stretch of the actual Tuscany Trail, or want a custom mix of the smoother Strade Bianche sectors and the rougher Maremma terrain, we're also happy to design a fully custom tour around this.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is this the official Tuscany Trail?

No. Our Tuscany Gravel Tour is not the official Tuscany Trail event or route. It is an independent, fully supported cycling holiday inspired by some of the most spectacular gravel roads found along the Tuscany Trail, combined with our own carefully selected routes.

Do I need bikepacking experience?

No.

title.raw: Raid Alps Cycling Tour: Geneva to Nice
title.rendered: Raid Alps Cycling Tour: Geneva to Nice

content.raw:
For riders who dream of crossing the Alps rather than simply riding in them, our Raid Alps is the ultimate challenge.

Unlike our single-base tours, this is a true point-to-point journey, starting in Geneva, Switzerland, and finishing on the Mediterranean coast in Nice, France. Over several unforgettable days, you'll ride through three Alpine countries, conquer some of cycling's most legendary mountain passes, and experience the changing landscapes, cultures and cuisine that make the Alps one of the world's greatest cycling destinations.

It's the most ambitious road cycling tour we offer.

What Is the Raid Alps?

The Raid Alps is a fully supported multi-day cycling journey linking the greatest climbs of Switzerland, Italy and France into one continuous adventure.

Rather than returning to the same hotel each evening, you'll finish every stage in a new destination as you steadily make your way south towards the Mediterranean.

Every itinerary is custom built, allowing us to match the route to your available time, fitness level and the climbs you've always wanted to ride.

A Typical Route

While every Raid Alps is tailored to each group, a classic Geneva to Nice itinerary may include iconic climbs such as:

  • The Col de la Colombière
  • Col des Aravis
  • Cormet de Roselend
  • Col de l'Iseran, the highest paved mountain pass in the Alps
  • Col du Galibier, one of cycling's greatest climbs
  • Col d'Izoard
  • Col de Vars
  • Col de la Bonette, the highest paved road in France
  • Col de la Cayolle
  • The legendary Col de la Madone
  • A spectacular finish overlooking the Mediterranean in Nice

Every edition is different, with routes adapted to the group's ambitions, weather conditions and desired daily distances.

Why Choose a Point-to-Point Tour?

Most cycling holidays are based in one location, allowing riders to explore nearby climbs before returning to the same hotel each evening.

The Raid Alps offers something completely different.

Every day brings new roads, new scenery and a new destination. Instead of riding loops, you'll experience the satisfaction of genuinely crossing one of Europe's greatest mountain ranges from north to south.

It feels less like a cycling holiday and more like a true expedition.

Fitness Requirements

This is our most demanding road cycling tour.

Expect consecutive days of long mountain climbs, significant elevation gain and limited recovery between stages. Riders should already be comfortable spending multiple hours climbing and ideally have previous experience riding in the Alps.

If you're unsure whether it's the right challenge, our Fitness Levels Guide can help you decide.

Full Support Throughout the Journey

A ride of this scale requires careful planning, allowing you to focus entirely on enjoying the cycling.

Throughout the tour we provide:

  • Daily luggage transfers
  • Professional support vehicle
  • Mechanical assistance
  • Nutrition and feed stops
  • Carefully selected hotels
  • Route planning and navigation
  • Experienced local knowledge

With logistics taken care of, you can simply enjoy riding some of the world's greatest roads.

Who Is This Tour For?

The Raid Alps is designed for experienced cyclists looking for the ultimate Alpine adventure.

It's perfect for riders who:

  • Have already completed several mountain sportives or Alpine holidays
  • Enjoy long days in the saddle
  • Want to experience multiple Alpine regions in one trip
  • Are looking for a once-in-a-lifetime cycling challenge

Whether you're riding with friends, a cycling club or organising a private group, every Raid Alps itinerary is built specifically for you.

Plan Your Own Raid Alps

Every Raid Alps tour is custom designed.

We'll discuss your available dates, preferred daily distances, must-ride climbs and overall goals before creating a bespoke itinerary from Geneva to Nice that suits your group.

Our team handles the hotels, transfers, support vehicle and logistics so you can simply enjoy the ride.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many days does a typical Raid Alps take?
This varies significantly by route and group ambition, but most versions run 5-8 riding days to link a meaningful sequence of major climbs without excessive daily distances.

Do I need to have done a standard Cigala Alps tour before attempting this?
Not strictly required, but strongly recommended — the cumulative demand of consecutive major climbs is considerably higher than a single-base tour, and prior experience with at least one big Alpine climb helps set realistic expectations.

Does the Raid Alps cross international borders?
Depending on the specific route chosen, yes — versions incorporating the Swiss passes or finishing on the Italian side of the Stelvio involve border crossings, which we handle as part of the logistics planning.

Is this available as a fixed departure, or always custom?
Always custom, given the number of possible route combinations and the need to match the itinerary to a specific group's timeframe and climbing priorities.

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours

title.raw: Cycling Alpe d'Huez: Complete Guide
title.rendered: Cycling Alpe d’Huez: Complete Guide

content.raw:
No climb in cycling has quite the same cultural weight as Alpe d'Huez. The 21 numbered hairpins, each bearing the name of a Tour de France stage winner who triumphed there, have turned this from a simple mountain road into something closer to a pilgrimage site for cyclists. I've ridden it more times than I can count, and the atmosphere on race weekend — thousands of fans lining every hairpin — is genuinely unlike anywhere else in cycling.

Key Numbers

  • Length: 13.8km from Bourg d'Oisans
  • Average gradient: 8.1%
  • Elevation gain: approximately 1,071m
  • Summit elevation: 1,860m
  • The 21 hairpins: numbered in descending order as you climb, so hairpin 21 is near the bottom and hairpin 1 is at the very top — a small but genuinely motivating detail once you understand it

A Brief History

Alpe d'Huez first appeared in the Tour de France in 1952, when Fausto Coppi won the first-ever mountaintop finish here. It disappeared from the race for over two decades before returning in 1976 and has been a fixture ever since, hosting more mountaintop finishes than almost any other climb in the sport. The tradition of naming each hairpin after a stage winner began later and has become one of the most recognizable pieces of cycling folklore — riding past hairpin 7, for instance, and knowing which rider's name is painted there, adds a layer of history to every kilometre.t, with routes adapted to the group's ambitions, weather conditions and desired daily distances.

What Makes It Different From Other Famous Climbs

Unlike the Galibier or Stelvio, which feel remote and high-altitude, Alpe d'Huez has a resort town at the summit, meaning the climb ends not at a bare mountain pass but among hotels, shops, and the general infrastructure of a ski resort in its summer mode. This changes the character of the ride — less wilderness, more spectacle, especially with the fan graffiti painted on the road surface that builds up before each Tour de France visit and lingers for years afterward.

Difficulty in Context

The average gradient of 8.1% is genuinely tough and rarely lets up — unlike some longer climbs with gentler sections to recover on, Alpe d'Huez maintains a fairly relentless pitch throughout, with the first few kilometres from Bourg d'Oisans actually the steepest section of the entire climb, which surprises many first-timers expecting an easier start.

Best Time to Ride

June through September offers the most reliable conditions. Race weekend itself (when the Tour de France visits, which isn't every year) draws enormous crowds of amateur riders attempting the climb in the days before the professionals, which some riders love for the atmosphere and others prefer to avoid for the traffic and congestion on the road.

Tips From the Road

Pace yourself against the hairpin markers rather than the summit — with 21 numbered turns counting down, it's easy to break the effort into manageable chunks rather than fixating on the total distance remaining. The steep opening kilometres catch many first-timers out; resist the urge to match a strong start with an equally strong middle section, since the gradient doesn't meaningfully ease until near the top.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

Alpe d'Huez is one of the centerpiece climbs on our French Alps cycling tour, and it also features as one of the possible stops on a custom Raid Alps traverse for riders wanting to link it with other major Alpine climbs.

If you'd like this climb combined with other regional favorites or timed around a specific Tour de France visit, we're also happy to design a fully custom tour around it.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Alpe d'Huez harder than the Galibier or Stelvio?
It's shorter than both, but its relentless, unrelieved gradient makes it feel similarly demanding despite the lower total elevation gain — a different kind of hard rather than simply easier.

How busy is the road with tourist traffic?
Reasonably busy in peak summer given the resort town at the summit, though nowhere near as congested as during an actual Tour de France visit, when amateur ride days draw enormous numbers of cyclists.

Can beginners attempt Alpe d'Huez?
A rider comfortable sustaining a hard effort for around an hour can complete it, though the consistent steep gradient makes it a genuine test even for reasonably fit recreational riders.

Is there anywhere to refuel partway up?
Limited options exist at a couple of the hairpin bends in season, but it's best treated as a self-supported effort with your own water and nutrition for the roughly hour-long climb.

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours

title.raw: Cycling Ireland's Wild Atlantic Way: A Rider's Guide
title.rendered: Cycling Ireland’s Wild Atlantic Way: A Rider’s Guide

content.raw:
Ireland is the outlier in our destination list — no mountain passes chasing Giro or Tour de France history, no Mediterranean gravel. What it offers instead is something genuinely rare in European cycling: wild, dramatic coastal scenery with very little traffic, and a character of riding unlike anywhere else we operate.

The Wild Atlantic Way

Our Ireland routes draw heavily on sections of the Wild Atlantic Way, the signposted touring route that traces almost the entire western Irish coastline from Donegal to Cork. It's one of the longest defined coastal driving and cycling routes in the world, and riding sections of it puts you on genuinely quiet roads with the raw Atlantic on one side and green countryside on the other.

What the Terrain Is Actually Like

Expect rolling, occasionally punchy terrain rather than sustained climbing — short, sharp rises as roads cross headlands, interspersed with flatter coastal and valley stretches. Nothing here matches Alpine gradients, but the constant undulation and, more significantly, the wind, make for a more demanding ride than the elevation profile alone would suggest.

Weather and Wind

This is the single biggest factor to plan around in Ireland, more than in almost any other destination we operate. Atlantic weather systems bring genuine variability — sun, rain, and wind can all arrive within the same afternoon, and a strong headwind off the ocean can slow progress more than any hill. Packing for changeable conditions matters more here than for our Mediterranean destinations, regardless of season.

Best Time to Ride

May through September offers the most reliable weather, with June and July typically driest, though "reliable" in an Irish context still means packing for rain regardless of forecast. The extended daylight hours in early summer are a genuine bonus, with light lingering well into the evening.

What Makes Ireland Worth It

Beyond the riding itself, the culture along the way is a real draw — small coastal villages with genuinely warm hospitality, traditional music in local pubs after a day's ride, and a slower pace than the more cycling-tourism-developed regions of continental Europe. Riders who come for the roads often say the evenings are just as memorable.

Common Mistakes First-Timers Make

Underestimating wind is the most common one — a forecast that looks entirely manageable on paper can produce a genuinely tough headwind section along an exposed headland. The second is under-packing for rain, assuming a sunny forecast will hold for the whole day; Irish weather changes faster than that.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

Every one of our Ireland cycling tours is fully custom. Whether you're looking for a relaxed coastal escape, an epic point-to-point adventure, or a route linking Ireland's most iconic climbs and landscapes, we'll design the itinerary around your group's goals, fitness level, preferred daily distances, and travel dates. No two tours have to be the same. Get in touch with us to design a fully custom tour around Ireland for your group.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Ireland a good destination for climbing-focused riders?
Not in the Alpine sense — there's no sustained high-mountain climbing here. The challenge comes from wind, distance, and constantly undulating terrain rather than single big climbs.

What's the best month to avoid rain?
No month guarantees dry weather in Ireland, but May and June tend to be the driest on average — pack for rain regardless of when you travel.

Is this a good trip for a mixed-ability group?
Yes — the terrain's moderate, rolling character suits a broad range of fitness levels better than our high-mountain destinations do.

How does Ireland compare to Croatia's coastal riding?
Croatia offers warmer, more reliably dry Mediterranean conditions with an island-hopping element; Ireland trades that for wilder, more dramatic Atlantic scenery and a distinctly different cultural experience along the way.

title.rendered: Cycling Girona: Inside the Pro Peloton’s Favorite Town

content.raw:
If Mallorca and Calpe are where professional teams go for winter training camps, Girona is where a remarkable number of professional cyclists actually live year-round. This medieval Catalan town has become one of the most concentrated hubs of professional cycling talent anywhere in the world, and riding its surrounding roads means genuinely following in the daily training routes of some of the sport's biggest names.

Why Girona Became Cycling's Adopted Home

The reasons are practical rather than mysterious — a nearby international airport, a mild climate, genuinely excellent and varied riding terrain within a short radius, good food, and a lower cost of living than some other cycling hubs, combined with an early wave of professional riders settling here that snowballed into today's concentrated community. It's now common to share a café stop with riders you'd otherwise only see on television.

The Riding Terrain

Girona's surrounding countryside offers a genuinely rare combination — flat, fast valley roads for easy days, rolling countryside through the Catalan hinterland for moderate efforts, and access to real climbing in the nearby Pyrenean foothills and coastal Costa Brava hills for harder days, all without needing to relocate your base during a trip.

Rocacorba

The region's best-known local training climb, Rocacorba has become something of a proving ground among the resident professional community, with informal Strava-segment rivalries among some of the sport's biggest names adding a layer of cycling culture to what is, on paper, a moderate, well-surfaced climbing road through forested hills.

The Costa Brava Connection

Girona's proximity to the dramatic Costa Brava coastline means a day trip east brings you to genuinely different terrain — rugged coastal roads and small fishing villages, a contrasting change of scenery from the inland valleys and hills that dominate most Girona-based riding.

Café Culture and Cycling Community

Girona's cycling scene extends well beyond the roads themselves — a genuine café culture has developed around cyclist-friendly spots throughout town, and the general atmosphere of a place where cycling is simply part of daily life, rather than a niche tourist activity, is part of what makes basing a trip here feel different from a purely scenery-driven destination.

Gravel Cycling in Girona

While Girona is famous for its road cycling, it's equally renowned as one of Europe's best gravel riding destinations. Within minutes of leaving the city, smooth gravel tracks weave through forests, vineyards and quiet countryside, allowing riders to escape traffic almost immediately.

The region offers an incredible variety of terrain, from fast hard-packed gravel roads ideal for adventure bikes to more technical trails for experienced riders. Many of the world's top professional cyclists regularly include gravel rides in their training, and it's common to see riders swapping their road bikes for gravel bikes on recovery days or long endurance rides.

Popular routes head towards Els Àngels, the Gavarres Natural Park and the quiet gravel roads surrounding the medieval villages of Madremanya, Monells and Púbol. The network is so extensive that no two rides ever need to be the same.

Whether you're looking for a relaxed coffee ride or a full-day gravel adventure with over 2,500 metres of climbing, Girona offers some of the finest gravel cycling in Europe.

Best Time to Ride

Spring and autumn offer the most comfortable temperatures, though Girona's inland Catalan climate is milder than the deep Mediterranean heat found further south, making it a genuinely rideable destination across a longer season than some of our more southern options.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

Girona works well as a distinctive addition to our roster, offering genuine variety in terrain within a single base and a cycling culture unlike anywhere else we operate, rooted in the town's status as an adopted home for professional riders.

If you'd like an itinerary built around specific local climbs, the Costa Brava coastal option, or a longer stay soaking in the town's cycling culture, we're also happy to design a fully custom tour around Girona for your group.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will I actually see professional cyclists riding around Girona?
It's genuinely common, particularly during the European racing season when many residents are training locally between events, though obviously not guaranteed on any given day.

Is Girona better suited to climbing or flatter riding?
Both are genuinely available within a short radius — this variety within a single base is one of Girona's specific strengths compared to destinations built around one type of terrain.

How far is the Costa Brava coast from Girona?
Close enough for a full day-trip ride there and back, or a one-way route with vehicle support for the return, making it an easy addition to a Girona-based week.

Is Girona good for gravel cycling?

Absolutely. Girona has become one of Europe's leading gravel destinations, with hundreds of kilometres of well-maintained gravel roads and forest tracks starting just outside the city. Whether you ride road, gravel or both, Girona offers exceptional terrain for every type of cyclist.

Is Girona a good base for a custom trip combining cycling with general travel?
Yes — the town's own historic old quarter and the wider Catalan region offer plenty for non-riding time, making it a well-rounded base beyond just the cycling itself.

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours

title.raw: Cycling Mallorca: Why the Pros Train Here
title.rendered: Cycling Mallorca: Why the Pros Train Here

content.raw:
Mallorca has been the training-camp island of choice for professional cycling teams for decades, and once you've ridden it, the reason is obvious — a genuinely rare combination of reliable early-season weather, excellent road surfaces, and a range of terrain from flat coastal spins to serious mountain climbing, all within a compact island you can cross in a day.

Why Pro Teams Choose Mallorca

Every winter and early spring, the island fills with professional teams doing their base training, drawn by mild Mediterranean temperatures when much of continental Europe is still cold, combined with genuinely good climbing terrain in the Serra de Tramuntana mountain range along the northwest coast. This isn't a marketing angle — it's a well-established fact of the professional cycling calendar, and riding the same roads as WorldTour teams in February is part of Mallorca's appeal.

Sa Calobra: The Signature Climb

No Mallorca guide is complete without Sa Calobra, one of the most distinctive climbs in Europe — around 10km with roughly 26 numbered hairpins, including the famous 270-degree "tie knot" loop partway up where the road literally passes back under itself. It's not the longest or steepest climb on the island, but it's unforgettable, dropping from the Tramuntana ridge down to a small cove on the coast, meaning most riders climb it in the "wrong" direction from the sea back up to the main road.

Puig Major

The island's highest paved climb, Puig Major offers a longer, more sustained test than Sa Calobra, climbing through the same Tramuntana range with genuinely mountainous scenery despite the island setting — a reminder that Mallorca's climbing is a legitimate mountain-cycling experience, not just a beach-holiday add-on.

The Rest of the Island

Beyond the Tramuntana climbs, Mallorca offers flat, fast coastal roads perfect for easier days or recovery rides, plus a network of quiet inland roads through almond and olive groves in the island's agricultural heartland — genuine variety within a single, compact destination.

Best Time to Ride

October through May is the prime cycling season, precisely because it avoids the intense summer heat and tourist crowds of the beach season — this inverse seasonality compared to most of our Mediterranean destinations is part of what makes Mallorca such a valuable addition to a touring calendar, filling exactly the months when Alpine and Pyrenean high passes are closed.

Bike Choice

A road bike is the right tool for essentially the entire island — Mallorca's cycling infrastructure is built around road riding, with excellent tarmac throughout, and there's little reason to bring a gravel setup here unless specifically seeking out the island's more remote agricultural back roads.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

Mallorca is one of our favorite off-season additions precisely because it fills the winter and early spring gap left by our higher-altitude destinations, offering genuine mountain climbing in the Tramuntana alongside easy coastal days, all in reliably mild weather.

If you'd like a custom itinerary focused specifically on Sa Calobra and Puig Major, or want to combine mountain days with more relaxed coastal riding, we're also happy to design a fully custom tour around Mallorca for your group.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Mallorca only good for winter training, or is it worth visiting in other seasons?
Winter and spring are the standout seasons given the mild climate and quiet roads; summer is rideable but hot and considerably busier with general tourism.

How does Sa Calobra compare in difficulty to Alpine climbs like Alpe d'Huez?
Shorter and less demanding overall, though the tie-knot hairpin and consistently technical descent-then-climb structure make it a genuinely memorable, moderately challenging ride rather than an easy spin.

Do professional teams actually train on the same roads tourists ride?
Yes — this is one of the more unusual aspects of Mallorca cycling; the Tramuntana roads used by WorldTour teams for winter training camps are entirely open public roads.

Is Mallorca suitable for a mixed-ability group?
Very much so — the combination of serious mountain climbing and easy flat coastal roads within a compact island makes it one of our more flexible destinations for groups with a range of fitness levels.

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours

Alongside Mallorca, Calpe on Spain's Costa Blanca has become one of Europe's other major winter cycling hubs, drawing professional teams and serious amateur riders alike for the same reasons — reliable mild weather, excellent roads, and genuine climbing terrain within easy reach of the coast.

Why Calpe Specifically

Calpe's appeal comes from its position at the base of the Costa Blanca's inland mountains, with the dramatic Peñón de Ifach rock formation marking the town itself, and a network of climbing roads reaching into the hills within a short ride of the coast. Unlike some coastal training destinations, you don't need a long transfer to reach genuine climbing — it starts almost immediately inland from town.

The Coll de Rates

The region's best-known climb, the Coll de Rates is a moderate, well-surfaced ascent through orange groves and almond trees, popular enough with training cyclists that it's rarely quiet, but rightly so — consistent gradient, excellent road surface, and genuinely scenic climbing through Mediterranean agricultural terrain.

Beyond the Coll de Rates

The wider Costa Blanca hinterland offers considerably more climbing than just this one signature road — a network of interconnected valley and mountain roads means multi-day itineraries here rarely repeat the same route twice, with options ranging from gentle valley rides to more serious sustained climbs further inland.

Best Time to Ride

Similar to Mallorca, October through April is prime season, avoiding the intense summer heat that makes inland climbing genuinely uncomfortable in July and August. Winter here stays notably mild even by Mediterranean standards, which is precisely why the professional training-camp culture developed around this coast.

What Makes This Different From Mallorca

Where Mallorca is an island with a defined, compact geography, the Costa Blanca is part of the Spanish mainland, meaning the climbing terrain extends further inland with more variety and, generally, fewer other cyclists sharing the most popular roads compared to Mallorca's more concentrated, internationally famous climbs.

Bike Choice

A road bike is the right tool for essentially the entire island — Mallorca's cycling infrastructure is built around road riding, with excellent tarmac throughout, and there's little reason to bring a gravel setup here unless specifically seeking out the island's more remote agricultural back roads.

Frequently Asked Questions

How does Calpe compare to Mallorca for a winter training trip?
Both offer similarly mild winter weather and genuine climbing; Calpe's mainland location offers somewhat more extensive and less crowded inland terrain, while Mallorca has the more internationally recognized signature climbs.

Is the Coll de Rates suitable for less experienced climbers?
Yes — it's a moderate, consistent climb well suited to riders building confidence on sustained ascents, without the more extreme gradients found on some Alpine climbs.

What's the coastal town of Calpe itself like to stay in?
A pleasant, moderately sized coastal town with good infrastructure for cycling visitors, including the distinctive Peñón de Ifach rock formation as a local landmark.

Is this a good destination outside of the winter training season?
It's rideable year-round, but summer heat inland makes serious climbing days considerably less comfortable — winter and shoulder-season months remain the better choice.

content.raw:
Portugal's southern coast has quietly built a reputation among European cyclists as one of the best off-season destinations on the continent, and it's easy to see why once you've ridden it — reliably mild winter temperatures, genuinely good road surfaces, and rolling countryside that rewards exploration without demanding Alpine-level fitness.

What the Terrain Is Actually Like

The Algarve's interior is more varied than its beach-resort reputation might suggest — rolling hills through cork oak forests and agricultural land, with occasional short, punchy climbs, rather than either flat coastal spinning or serious mountain terrain. It's genuinely approachable riding, well suited to building confidence or simply enjoying scenery without needing peak climbing fitness.

The Coastal Roads

Along the coast itself, quieter roads connect a string of towns and fishing villages, with dramatic limestone cliff scenery in the western Algarve around Sagres and Lagos contrasting with the flatter, more developed eastern stretches nearer Faro. The western coast, less built up than the busier central Algarve resorts, tends to offer the quieter, more scenic riding.

Why Winter Works So Well Here

Much like Cyprus and Mallorca, the Algarve's appeal for cyclists is largely about timing — daytime temperatures through winter typically sit in a comfortable mid-teens to high-teens Celsius range, a genuine escape when much of northern and central Europe is cold and grey, without the intense heat that makes summer riding here considerably less pleasant.

Food and Culture

Portuguese cuisine along this coast leans heavily on excellent fresh seafood, and the pace of life in the smaller Algarve towns rewards slowing down after a ride — a noticeably different rhythm from busier Mediterranean tourist destinations, even in the region's own high season.

Best Time to Ride

October through April is the sweet spot, mirroring the same logic that makes Cyprus and Mallorca appealing off-season destinations — comfortable riding temperatures precisely when the rest of Europe's cycling regions are closed for winter or uncomfortably cold.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

Our Algarve cycling tour is built around this rolling coastal and inland terrain, timed for the cooler months when the region is at its cycling best, with daily distances that suit riders across a broad range of fitness levels.

If you'd like a different balance of coastal versus inland riding, or want to combine the Algarve with another Iberian destination, we're also happy to design a fully custom tour around this region for your group.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Algarve suitable for beginner cyclists?
Yes — the rolling, moderate terrain here is one of our more approachable destinations, without the sustained climbing demands of our Alpine or Pyrenean tours.

How does the Algarve compare to Cyprus or Mallorca as a winter destination?
All three share the same core appeal of mild winter weather; the Algarve's terrain is generally gentler than Cyprus's Troodos mountains or Mallorca's Tramuntana range, making it a good fit for riders prioritizing comfort over serious climbing.

Is the western or eastern Algarve better for cycling?
The western Algarve, around Sagres and Lagos, tends to offer quieter roads and more dramatic coastal scenery than the busier, more developed eastern stretches near Faro.

What's the water temperature like if I want to combine riding with a coastal holiday?
Winter Atlantic water here is considerably cooler than the Mediterranean, so this is more a riding-and-scenery destination in the cooler months than a swimming-focused trip.

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours

title.raw: Cycling the Swiss Alps: Grimsel, Furka, and Susten
title.rendered: Cycling the Swiss Alps: Grimsel, Furka, and Susten

content.raw:
Switzerland does mountain roads differently from its neighbors — impeccably engineered, immaculately maintained, and often threaded together into loops that let you link several major passes in a single big day, something that's harder to achieve in the more sprawling French or Italian Alps.

The Grimsel, Furka, and Susten Loop

These three passes, all in the Bernese Oberland and central Swiss Alps region, are often ridden together as a single legendary loop, sometimes called the "three passes" route by Swiss cyclists. Each has its own character: the Furka is famous partly for its James Bond film heritage (the Goldfinger car chase was filmed here) and offers dramatic views toward the Rhône Glacier; the Grimsel is a broader, more open high-altitude crossing; and the Susten, arguably the most scenic of the three, threads through dramatic granite scenery with a long, well-engineered ascent.

Why Swiss Roads Feel Different

Switzerland's famously meticulous infrastructure extends fully to its mountain roads — consistently excellent surfaces, clear signage, and a level of maintenance that makes even the most remote high passes feel considerably safer and more predictable than comparable roads elsewhere in the Alps. This precision comes at a cost, quite literally — Switzerland is an expensive country to travel in, which is worth factoring into trip planning.

Key Numbers

  • Grimsel Pass: summit at 2,164m
  • Furka Pass: summit at 2,429m
  • Susten Pass: summit at 2,224m

Linking all three in a single big loop is a genuine achievement, typically requiring a long day or split across two, given the combined distance and elevation gain involved.

Weather Considerations

As with any high Alpine pass, conditions at these altitudes change quickly, and all three passes are only open in the warmer months — generally June through October, subject to snowfall — with snow poles still visible alongside the road well into summer as a reminder of how much snow these routes see in winter.

Best Time to Ride

July and August offer the most reliable weather for tackling all three passes in a single ambitious day, though June and September offer quieter roads if you're comfortable with a slightly higher chance of a pass still being partially affected by late or early snow.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

The Swiss passes work particularly well as one stage of a longer custom Raid Alps traverse, linking with French or Italian Alpine climbs on either side, given Switzerland's central position within the wider Alpine range.

If you'd like a dedicated trip focused specifically on the Grimsel-Furka-Susten loop, or want it combined with neighboring regions, we're also happy to design a fully custom tour around Switzerland for your group.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can all three passes genuinely be ridden in a single day?
Yes, though it makes for a very long, demanding day given the combined distance and elevation — many riders prefer to split the loop across two days to enjoy each pass properly.

How does Switzerland compare in cost to French or Italian Alpine destinations?
Noticeably more expensive across accommodation, food, and general costs — worth factoring into budget expectations for a Switzerland-focused trip.

Is the Furka Pass really the one from the James Bond film?
Yes — the Furka Pass road featured in the 1964 film Goldfinger's car chase sequence, and it remains a point of interest for visiting cyclists and film fans alike.

What's the best base town for riding this loop?
Towns in the Bernese Oberland or the Uri canton near the base of these passes make practical starting points, chosen based on which direction you plan to tackle the loop.

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours

title.raw: Cycling Slovenia: The Julian Alps and Vršič Pass
title.rendered: Cycling Slovenia: The Julian Alps and Vršič Pass

content.raw:
Slovenia is one of the quieter gems in European cycling, and I mean that literally — the roads through the Julian Alps carry a fraction of the traffic you'd find on comparable Italian or French passes, while offering scenery and climbing that rivals the more famous ranges next door.

The Julian Alps

This compact mountain range in Slovenia's northwest, extending into Italy, offers genuinely dramatic Alpine scenery — turquoise glacial rivers, sheer limestone peaks, and forested valleys — combined with a network of climbing roads considerably less discovered by international cycling tourism than equivalent terrain in the Dolomites or French Alps.

The Vršič Pass

Slovenia's signature climb and the highest paved mountain pass in the country, the Vršič connects the Soča Valley to the Sava Valley via a dramatic series of hairpins on both sides — 24 numbered switchbacks on the northern ascent alone. Built originally during the First World War for military purposes, it retains a slightly wilder, less manicured character than some of its more tourist-developed Alpine counterparts, with a gravel-surfaced section on part of the historic route still visible alongside the modern paved road.

The Soča Valley

On the western side of the pass, the Soča Valley offers some of the most strikingly colored river scenery in Europe — a genuinely turquoise glacial river running through a valley that also saw significant First World War fighting, adding a layer of history to what is already spectacular riding terrain.

Why Slovenia Stays Quiet

Despite offering climbing and scenery genuinely comparable to the Dolomites or parts of the French Alps, Slovenia simply hasn't developed the same international cycling-tourism profile, which works entirely in visiting cyclists' favor — quieter roads, less competition for accommodation, and a more relaxed atmosphere throughout.

Best Time to Ride

June through September, similar to other Alpine-altitude destinations, with the Vršič Pass itself subject to the same late-spring snow clearance timing as comparable high passes elsewhere in the Alps.

Gravel Riding in Slovenia

While Slovenia is renowned for its mountain roads, it's equally impressive for gravel cycling. A vast network of forest roads, military tracks, alpine plateaus, and quiet countryside lanes provides endless opportunities for adventure away from traffic.

From flowing gravel through Triglav National Park to hidden climbs above the Soča Valley and scenic routes linking remote mountain villages, Slovenia offers the perfect mix of challenging terrain and breathtaking scenery. Whether you're looking for smooth hard-packed gravel suitable for any gravel bike or more adventurous backcountry routes, there's something for every rider.

Our custom Slovenia tours can combine iconic road climbs like the Vršič Pass with unforgettable gravel adventures, creating a unique cycling experience that showcases the very best of this remarkable country.

Food and Culture

Slovenian cuisine blends Alpine, Mediterranean, and Balkan influences depending on the region, and the country's approachable size means a cycling trip here can combine mountain days with easy access to Lake Bled's famous scenery or the capital Ljubljana's compact, walkable old town.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

Slovenia is a genuine hidden-gem addition to our Alpine offerings, giving riders who've done the Dolomites or French Alps a comparably spectacular but considerably quieter alternative, centered on the Vršič Pass and Soča Valley.

If you'd like this combined with the neighboring Italian Dolomites given their geographic proximity, or want a custom itinerary focused specifically on the Julian Alps, we're also happy to design a fully custom tour for your group whether is road or gravel.

Frequently Asked Questions

How does the Vršič Pass compare to Italian Dolomites climbs?
Comparable in scenery and difficulty, but considerably quieter in terms of traffic and tourist crowds, which many experienced Alpine cyclists specifically seek out.

Is Slovenia easy to combine with a Dolomites or Italian Alps trip?
Yes, given its geographic proximity — this is one of the more natural custom combinations we build for riders wanting two distinct Alpine experiences in one trip.

What's the historical significance of the Vršič Pass?
It was built during the First World War for military logistics, and sections of the historic route, including some original construction, remain visible alongside the modern road.

Is Slovenia good for gravel cycling?

Absolutely. Slovenia is one of Europe's best gravel cycling destinations, with hundreds of kilometres of forest roads, alpine tracks, and quiet backroads. Our custom tours can include everything from scenic gravel routes suitable for first-time gravel riders to more technical mountain adventures for experienced cyclists.

Is Slovenia suitable for riders who don't want extreme climbing difficulty?
The Vršič is a genuine high-mountain pass and should be treated with the same respect as comparable Alpine climbs, though Slovenia's valleys also offer gentler riding for those wanting to balance harder days with easier ones.

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours

title.raw: Italy Coast to Coast: A Cycling Traverse
title.rendered: Italy Coast to Coast: A Cycling Traverse

content.raw:
There's something genuinely satisfying about a point-to-point journey that ends somewhere entirely different from where it began, and an Italy coast-to-coast crossing — from the Tyrrhenian Sea in the west to the Adriatic in the east, or vice versa — delivers exactly that, cutting through the country's varied heart rather than looping back to a single base.

What This Route Actually Covers

Unlike our region-specific tours, which explore outward from one base, the coast-to-coast concept is built around genuine point-to-point progression across Italy's width, typically through the central regions where the peninsula narrows enough to make the crossing achievable over a realistic number of riding days. Depending on the exact route, this can pass through Tuscany, Umbria, or the Marche, crossing the spine of the Apennines somewhere along the way.

The Apennines Crossing

The central mountain range running the length of Italy, the Apennines are less internationally famous than the Alps but offer genuine, substantial climbing — generally not reaching Alpine altitudes, but with a wilder, less-touristed character and roads that see a fraction of the traffic found on comparable Alpine passes.

Why This Route Appeals

The variety is the point — coastal riding on both ends, genuine mountain crossing in the middle, and the cultural range of central Italy along the way, from hill towns to countryside vineyards to smaller cities rarely visited by international tourists compared to Italy's more famous destinations. It's a rare chance to see the country's geography change meaningfully day by day rather than exploring a single region in depth.

Logistics of a Point-to-Point Route

Because you're finishing somewhere entirely different from where you start, logistics matter more here than for a standard loop-based tour — support vehicle routing, luggage transfer, and return transport from the finish all need proper planning, which is exactly why this works best as a custom-built itinerary tailored to a group's specific timeframe and starting/finishing preferences.

Best Time to Ride

Spring (April–June) and autumn (September–October) suit this route particularly well, avoiding both the crossing's higher-altitude sections being snow-affected and the lower coastal and valley sections becoming uncomfortably hot in peak summer.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

We have a specific Italy's Coast to Coast trip running every year.
Also, an Italy coast-to-coast crossing is one of our signature custom-built itineraries, drawing on the same central Italian terrain we know well from our Tuscany routes but extending the concept into a genuine point-to-point journey across the country's width.

Given the route's flexibility in exact start and finish points, this is always designed as a fully custom tour around your group's specific timeframe and preferences.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many days does a typical Italy coast-to-coast crossing take?
This varies by exact route and starting/finishing points, but most versions run 5-7 riding days to cross the peninsula's width at a reasonable, enjoyable pace.

Does this route require serious mountain-climbing fitness?
The Apennines crossing is genuinely demanding but generally doesn't reach the sustained high-altitude difficulty of an Alpine pass — a solid, fit recreational rider can manage it with reasonable preparation.

Which coast is the better starting point?
Either direction works well; the choice often comes down to travel logistics — which coast is more convenient to reach and depart from given your group's travel plans.

Is this route available as a fixed departure, or always custom?
Always custom, given the number of possible starting and finishing point combinations and the logistics involved in a genuine point-to-point journey.

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours

title.raw: Cycling Puglia: Italy's Flat, Sunny Heel
title.rendered: Cycling Puglia: Italy’s Flat, Sunny Heel

content.raw:
If Tuscany and the Dolomites represent Italy's rolling hills and high mountains, Puglia — the country's southern "heel" — offers something entirely different: predominantly flat to gently rolling terrain, ancient olive groves stretching to the horizon, and a distinctly different, sun-baked Mediterranean character from northern and central Italy.

What the Terrain Is Actually Like

This is genuinely some of the flattest riding terrain in our entire Italian portfolio — long, straight roads through olive groves that in places are centuries old, interrupted occasionally by the whitewashed hill towns and coastal stretches that punctuate the otherwise gentle landscape. It's a refreshing contrast for riders who've done our more mountainous Italian tours and want an easier-paced, high-mileage style of trip instead.

The Trulli Country

The Valle d'Itria region is home to Puglia's famous trulli — distinctive whitewashed conical-roofed stone huts unique to this part of Italy, clustered particularly around the town of Alberobello. Riding through this landscape, past centuries-old olive trees and these unusual traditional structures, gives Puglia a visual character genuinely unlike anywhere else in the country.

The Coastline

Puglia has two coasts — the Adriatic to the east and the Ionian to the west — both offering scenic coastal riding, with the Adriatic side generally better known for its dramatic cliffs and clear water, particularly around the Gargano promontory in the north of the region.

Best Time to Ride

Spring (April–May) and autumn (September–October) are ideal, avoiding the intense summer heat that makes flat, shade-free Puglian roads considerably less comfortable in July and August. The region's southern latitude means summer heat here can be more punishing than in northern or central Italy.

Food and Culture

Puglia has developed a genuine culinary reputation in its own right — excellent olive oil (the region produces a significant share of Italy's total production), orecchiette pasta, and burrata cheese, all best enjoyed at a relaxed pace after an easier riding day than our mountain-focused tours demand.

Why This Appeals to a Different Kind of Rider

Puglia suits riders prioritizing distance, scenery, and food over serious climbing — a genuinely different holiday style from our Alpine or Pyrenean tours, better compared to Croatia or the Algarve in terms of overall demand, though with its own distinct flat, olive-grove character.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

Puglia is a strong option for riders wanting an easier-paced Italian trip, or as a complementary addition for groups who've already done one of our more mountainous Italian destinations and want contrast on a return visit.

If you'd like this combined with a coast-to-coast Italy concept or want a custom mix of Adriatic and Ionian coastal riding, we're also happy to design a fully custom tour around Puglia for your group.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Puglia suitable for beginner cyclists?
Yes, very much so — the flat to gently rolling terrain here is among the most approachable in our entire portfolio, well suited to riders newer to multi-day touring.

How does Puglia compare to Tuscany?
Tuscany offers rolling hills and, on our gravel tour, unpaved sectors; Puglia is flatter and features distinctive trulli architecture and olive grove landscapes rather than Tuscany's vineyard hill country.

What's the cycling distance like on a typical Puglia day?
Generally longer daily distances than our mountain tours, given the flatter terrain — riders often cover more ground per day here with less overall fatigue than an equivalent mountain day would produce.

Is Puglia a good destination for combining cycling with food-focused travel?
Very much so — the region's culinary reputation is a genuine highlight, and the easier riding pace leaves more energy and appetite for the food and wine along the way.

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours

title.raw: Cycling Sicily: Mount Etna and the Coast
title.rendered: Cycling Sicily: Mount Etna and the Coast

content.raw:
Sicily offers something no other Italian destination in our portfolio can — the chance to climb an active volcano. Mount Etna dominates the island's cycling reputation, but Sicily's appeal extends well beyond it, into genuinely varied coastal and hill terrain across the wider island.

Climbing Mount Etna

Europe's largest active volcano, Etna offers several route options up its lower and mid slopes (the very summit crater area is off-limits to casual cyclists for safety reasons, and access can change based on volcanic activity). The climbing here is genuinely unique — riding through changing vegetation zones from citrus groves at the base to bare volcanic rock higher up, with visible lava flows from past eruptions crossing the road in places, a stark, otherworldly landscape unlike any other climb in Europe.

What Makes Etna Different From Alpine Climbs

Beyond the obvious volcanic novelty, Etna's climbing character differs from Alpine passes in its surroundings — rather than pine forest and alpine meadow, you're riding through a landscape shaped by relatively recent geological activity, with the mountain's summit often visibly venting steam, a genuine reminder that this is an active, living volcano rather than a dormant peak.

The Wider Island

Sicily is far more than just Etna — the island's coastline offers dramatic cliff-top roads and small fishing towns, particularly along the northern coast, while the interior hill country provides rolling, less-touristed riding through countryside dotted with ancient Greek and Roman ruins, a reminder of the island's long history as a crossroads of Mediterranean civilizations.

Best Time to Ride

Spring (April–May) and autumn (September–October) offer the most comfortable temperatures, with summer heat, particularly at lower elevations away from Etna's cooling altitude, becoming genuinely intense in July and August.

A Note on Etna's Activity

As an active volcano, Etna does occasionally experience eruptive activity that can affect access to certain roads or areas — this is a normal part of planning a Sicily cycling trip, and current conditions are always checked before finalizing any Etna-inclusive itinerary.

Food and Culture

Sicilian cuisine reflects the island's layered history — Arab, Greek, Norman, and Spanish influences all show up in the local food, alongside excellent seafood and some of Italy's best citrus, grown in the fertile volcanic soil around Etna's base.

Gravel Riding in Sicily

Sicily is one of Italy's most exciting destinations for gravel cycling. The slopes of Mount Etna are crisscrossed with volcanic tracks, ancient lava roads, forest trails, and quiet gravel lanes that offer a completely different perspective of the mountain. Away from Etna, rolling white roads weave through vineyards, olive groves, and remote hilltop villages, creating endless opportunities for adventure far from traffic.
The Sicily divide route is also a popular crossing of sicily providing incredible gravel riding.

Whether you're looking for fast-flowing gravel suitable for all experience levels or more challenging volcanic terrain, Sicily delivers an unforgettable riding experience. Our custom tours can combine iconic road climbs with carefully selected gravel routes, giving riders the best of both worlds.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

Sicily is one of our most unique Italian destinations, combining the unforgettable experience of riding an active volcano with spectacular coastal roads, historic villages, and incredible gravel riding.

Every one of our Sicily tours is fully custom. Whether you're looking for a road-focused week centred around Mount Etna, a gravel adventure exploring Sicily's volcanic landscapes and countryside, or a combination of both, we'll design a fully custom tour around Sicily for your group.the perfect itinerary for your group.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can you actually ride all the way to Etna's summit?
No — the true summit crater area is restricted for safety given ongoing volcanic activity, but the lower and mid-slope climbing routes offer a substantial, genuinely dramatic ride well up the mountain.

Is Etna dangerous to cycle given it's an active volcano?
The routes used for cycling are well away from any immediate hazard under normal conditions, and access plans always account for current activity levels — this is routinely managed rather than a significant risk in practice.

How does Etna's climbing compare to Alpine passes?
Comparable in terms of physical demand on lower slope routes, but with an entirely different visual and geological character — volcanic rather than alpine scenery throughout.

Is Sicily good for gravel cycling?

Absolutely. Sicily offers an outstanding mix of volcanic gravel roads, forest tracks, countryside lanes, and quiet white roads. The Mount Etna region is particularly popular, allowing riders to combine world-class road climbs with unique off-road adventures through volcanic landscapes.

Is Sicily a good destination for combining cycling with historical sightseeing?
Very much so — the island's Greek, Roman, and later historical sites are a genuine highlight alongside the riding, making it well suited to a trip balancing cycling with broader cultural exploration.

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours
