title.raw: Cycling Sardinia: Italy's Rugged Island Escape
title.rendered: Cycling Sardinia: Italy’s Rugged Island Escape

content.raw:
Sardinia offers a genuinely different character from mainland Italy, and even from its island neighbor Sicily — a wilder, more sparsely populated landscape of granite mountains, dramatic coastline, and a distinct local culture with its own language and traditions, all wrapped in some of the cleanest, quietest cycling roads in the Mediterranean.

What the Terrain Is Actually Like

Sardinia's interior is genuinely mountainous in character, dominated by granite ranges like the Gennargentu massif, offering substantial climbing without ever quite reaching Alpine altitudes. The coastline, meanwhile, alternates between dramatic cliff sections, particularly along the eastern Ogliastra coast, and the wide, pale-sand beaches the island is famous for, especially around the northern Costa Smeralda.

Why Sardinia's Roads Are So Quiet

Sardinia has a notably lower population density than mainland Italy, and its road network reflects this — long stretches with genuinely minimal traffic, even along scenic coastal sections that would be considerably busier in more developed parts of the Mediterranean. This is one of the island's biggest draws for cyclists specifically seeking solitude alongside scenery.

The Granite Interior

Away from the coast, Sardinia's mountainous interior offers a genuinely different riding experience from its beach-resort reputation — winding roads through cork oak forest and exposed granite terrain, past small inland villages that see far fewer visitors than the coastal resorts, with a distinct Sardinian culture and cuisine that differs meaningfully from the rest of Italy.

The Coastline

Sardinia's coastal roads offer some of the most photogenic riding in the Mediterranean — the Costa Smeralda in the northeast is the most internationally famous and developed stretch, while the Ogliastra coast further south and east offers dramatic limestone cliffs and considerably fewer crowds.

Gravel Riding in Sardinia

Sardinia is one of Europe's hidden gems for gravel cycling. Beyond its quiet tarmac roads lies an extensive network of white gravel roads, forestry tracks, old shepherd trails, and historic mining routes that cross some of the island's wildest landscapes.

Ride through cork oak forests, remote mountain plateaus, rugged coastal cliffs, and traditional villages where traffic is almost non-existent. From the Supramonte mountains to the Ogliastra region and the island's spectacular southwest, Sardinia offers endless opportunities for gravel adventures that combine challenging riding with breathtaking scenery.

Whether you're looking for smooth gravel routes suitable for all abilities or more demanding backcountry terrain, our custom tours can blend iconic road rides with unforgettable off-road exploration.

Best Time to Ride

Spring (April–June) and autumn (September–October) are ideal, avoiding both the intense summer heat and the peak tourist season that brings considerably heavier traffic to the most popular coastal roads, particularly around the Costa Smeralda in July and August.

Food and Culture

Sardinian cuisine and culture stand notably apart from mainland Italian traditions — distinct pasta shapes like malloreddus, unique cheeses including the famous (and famously pungent) casu marzu, and a language, Sardinian, considered by linguists to be one of the closest living relatives to Latin among Romance languages, a genuine point of local pride.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

Sardinia offers a distinctive combination of genuine mountain climbing and dramatic, quiet coastal riding, appealing to cyclists wanting Mediterranean island scenery without the crowds found on some more internationally developed island destinations.

If you'd like an itinerary balanced toward the granite interior, the quieter Ogliastra coast, or a mix of both, or a multi-day gravel adventure we're also happy to design a fully custom tour around Sardinia for your group.

Frequently Asked Questions

How does Sardinia's climbing compare to the Alps or Sicily's Etna?
Genuinely substantial but generally not reaching Alpine altitudes — the granite interior offers real, sustained climbing without quite the sheer scale of the highest Alpine passes.

Is Sardinia quieter than Sicily for cycling?
Generally yes — Sardinia's lower population density and less internationally developed cycling-tourism profile mean quieter roads on average, particularly away from the busiest coastal resort areas.

What's the best coast to ride — Costa Smeralda or Ogliastra?
Costa Smeralda is the more famous, developed option; Ogliastra offers dramatic scenery with considerably fewer crowds, making it the choice for riders prioritizing solitude over polish.

Is Sardinia good for gravel cycling?

Absolutely. Sardinia is one of Italy's premier gravel destinations, offering hundreds of kilometres of white roads, forestry tracks, coastal trails, and mountain routes through some of the island's most remote landscapes. Our custom tours can include everything from scenic gravel adventures to more challenging multi-day off-road rides.

Is Sardinian cuisine very different from the rest of Italy?
Yes, meaningfully so — distinct pasta shapes, cheeses, and a unique local language all mark Sardinia as culturally distinct within Italy, adding genuine variety for riders who've done other Italian tours.

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours

title.raw: Cycling Corsica: Mountains Meet the Mediterranean
title.rendered: Cycling Corsica: Mountains Meet the Mediterranean

content.raw:
Corsica has a well-earned reputation as one of the most demanding, spectacular islands in the Mediterranean for cycling — a place where genuine high-mountain terrain drops almost directly into the sea, packed into an island you can cross in a single determined day.

Why Corsica Stands Out

Unlike most Mediterranean island destinations, which offer either coastal riding or moderate hills, Corsica gives you real mountains — the interior reaches over 2,700m at Monte Cinto, and the road network climbs deep into granite peaks that feel more like the Alps than a typical island getaway. The French Tour de France has started here three times, a recognition of how seriously the terrain is regarded within professional cycling.

The Col de Bavella

One of Corsica's signature climbs, the Col de Bavella winds through the dramatic Aiguilles de Bavella — a series of jagged granite spires that give this pass a genuinely otherworldly character, unlike anywhere else we operate. The climbing here is substantial without reaching the extreme altitude of the highest Alpine passes, but the scenery more than compensates.

Coastal Riding

Corsica's coastline is as varied as its interior — the western coast offers dramatic cliff-top roads with the famous red granite of the Calanques de Piana, while the eastern coast is flatter and faster, a good complement to harder mountain days.

A Distinct Culture

Corsica maintains a strong regional identity within France, with its own language and a cuisine that draws more from the wider Mediterranean and Italian tradition than mainland French cooking — chestnut-based dishes, local charcuterie, and excellent local wines feature heavily, and are worth building rest days around.

Best Time to Ride

May, June, and September are ideal — warm without the intense heat and heavier tourist traffic of July and August, when the island's beaches draw considerably more visitors and vehicle traffic on the coastal roads.

What Makes This Genuinely Demanding

The combination of altitude, heat (particularly at lower elevations in summer), and Corsica's famously winding, narrow mountain roads means this is one of our more physically demanding island destinations — closer in character to a compact Alpine trip than a typical Mediterranean island holiday.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

Corsica offers a rare combination of genuine mountain climbing and Mediterranean island scenery, appealing to riders who want Alpine-level challenge without leaving the coast entirely behind.

If you'd like an itinerary weighted toward the mountainous interior or the coastal roads, or want to combine both across a longer stay, we're also happy to design a fully custom tour around Corsica for your group.

Frequently Asked Questions

How does Corsica compare in difficulty to the French Alps?
Genuinely comparable in places — the interior climbs are substantial, though generally shorter than the biggest Alpine passes, with the added demand of heat at lower elevations.

Is Corsica a good destination for combining mountains and beach time?
Yes — this dual character is one of the island's defining strengths, letting a trip balance serious climbing days with coastal relaxation in a way few destinations manage.

What language is spoken in Corsica?
French is the official language, though Corsican, a distinct regional language related to Italian Tuscan dialects, remains widely spoken and a point of local cultural pride.

Is Corsica busy with tourists during peak cycling season?
Traffic increases in July and August, particularly on coastal roads, but the mountainous interior stays comparatively quiet even in peak summer.

— Matteo Cigala

Corsica has a well-earned reputation as one of the most demanding, spectacular islands in the Mediterranean for cycling — a place where genuine high-mountain terrain drops almost directly into the sea, packed into an island you can cross in a single determined day.

Why Corsica Stands Out

Unlike most Mediterranean island destinations, which offer either coastal riding or moderate hills, Corsica gives you real mountains — the interior reaches over 2,700m at Monte Cinto, and the road network climbs deep into granite peaks that feel more like the Alps than a typical island getaway. The French Tour de France has started here three times, a recognition of how seriously the terrain is regarded within professional cycling.

The Col de Bavella

One of Corsica’s signature climbs, the Col de Bavella winds through the dramatic Aiguilles de Bavella — a series of jagged granite spires that give this pass a genuinely otherworldly character, unlike anywhere else we operate. The climbing here is substantial without reaching the extreme altitude of the highest Alpine passes, but the scenery more than compensates.

Coastal Riding

Corsica’s coastline is as varied as its interior — the western coast offers dramatic cliff-top roads with the famous red granite of the Calanques de Piana, while the eastern coast is flatter and faster, a good complement to harder mountain days.

A Distinct Culture

Corsica maintains a strong regional identity within France, with its own language and a cuisine that draws more from the wider Mediterranean and Italian tradition than mainland French cooking — chestnut-based dishes, local charcuterie, and excellent local wines feature heavily, and are worth building rest days around.

Best Time to Ride

May, June, and September are ideal — warm without the intense heat and heavier tourist traffic of July and August, when the island’s beaches draw considerably more visitors and vehicle traffic on the coastal roads.

What Makes This Genuinely Demanding

The combination of altitude, heat (particularly at lower elevations in summer), and Corsica’s famously winding, narrow mountain roads means this is one of our more physically demanding island destinations — closer in character to a compact Alpine trip than a typical Mediterranean island holiday.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

Corsica offers a rare combination of genuine mountain climbing and Mediterranean island scenery, appealing to riders who want Alpine-level challenge without leaving the coast entirely behind.

If you’d like an itinerary weighted toward the mountainous interior or the coastal roads, or want to combine both across a longer stay, we’re also happy to design a fully custom tour around Corsica for your group.

Frequently Asked Questions

How does Corsica compare in difficulty to the French Alps?
Genuinely comparable in places — the interior climbs are substantial, though generally shorter than the biggest Alpine passes, with the added demand of heat at lower elevations.

Is Corsica a good destination for combining mountains and beach time?
Yes — this dual character is one of the island’s defining strengths, letting a trip balance serious climbing days with coastal relaxation in a way few destinations manage.

What language is spoken in Corsica?
French is the official language, though Corsican, a distinct regional language related to Italian Tuscan dialects, remains widely spoken and a point of local cultural pride.

Is Corsica busy with tourists during peak cycling season?
Traffic increases in July and August, particularly on coastal roads, but the mountainous interior stays comparatively quiet even in peak summer.

title.raw: Cycling Greece: Mountains, Islands, and Ancient Roads
title.rendered: Cycling Greece: Mountains, Islands, and Ancient Roads

content.raw:
Greece rarely tops European cycling destination lists, and that's a genuine oversight — the mainland's mountainous terrain, particularly in the Peloponnese, offers substantial climbing through landscapes layered with ancient history, largely bypassed by international cycling tourism.

The Peloponnese

This mountainous peninsula in southern mainland Greece offers the country's most rewarding cycling terrain — genuine climbing through olive groves and pine forest, connecting ancient sites like Mycenae, Epidaurus, and Olympia along quiet roads that see remarkably little traffic given their historical significance.

Mount Parnon and Mount Taygetus

The Peloponnese's mountain ranges offer real climbing substance — Taygetus in particular rises dramatically above Sparta, with roads winding through dense forest and offering some of the most rewarding sustained climbing found anywhere in Greece.

Island Options

Beyond the mainland, several Greek islands offer their own distinct cycling character — the terrain varies considerably by island, from the volcanic climbs of Santorini to the more substantial mountain roads of Crete, which has a genuinely serious interior mountain range reaching over 2,400m.

Why Greek Roads Stay Quiet

Greece simply hasn't developed the same international cycling-tourism infrastructure as Italy, France, or Spain, which works in visiting cyclists' favor — genuinely quiet roads, even around major historical sites that draw considerable general tourist traffic by car and coach.

Food and Culture

Greek cuisine needs little introduction — fresh seafood, excellent olive oil, and a genuinely relaxed, hospitable culture around meals that rewards a slower-paced touring style, well suited to a trip that balances riding with time at ancient sites along the way.

Best Time to Ride

April, May, and October are ideal — avoiding both the intense summer heat that makes climbing in exposed Mediterranean terrain genuinely uncomfortable and the peak tourist crowds at the country's most famous historical sites.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

Greece offers a genuinely distinctive addition to our roster, combining substantial mainland climbing with the option of island riding and a density of ancient historical sites unmatched by any of our other destinations.

If you'd like an itinerary focused on the Peloponnese, a specific island, or a mix of mainland and island riding, we're also happy to design a fully custom tour around Greece for your group.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is mainland Greece or a Greek island better for serious climbing?
The Peloponnese on the mainland generally offers more sustained, substantial climbing terrain; islands vary considerably, with Crete standing out for genuine mountain riding among the island options.

Can a Greece cycling trip include visits to ancient historical sites?
Very much so — this is one of the region's specific strengths, with sites like Mycenae, Epidaurus, and Olympia reachable directly by bike along the touring routes.

Is Greece a hot destination for cycling?
Summer heat is intense, particularly at lower elevations — spring and autumn are considerably more comfortable for serious riding days.

How does Greek cycling infrastructure compare to Italy or France?
Less internationally developed, meaning genuinely quiet roads, though also somewhat less specific cycling-tourism infrastructure — a trade-off that generally favors visiting cyclists seeking solitude.

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours

title.raw: Cycling the Canary Islands: Tenerife, Gran Canaria, and More
title.rendered: Cycling the Canary Islands: Tenerife, Gran Canaria, and More

content.raw:
The Canary Islands hold a unique position in the professional cycling calendar — genuinely year-round riding weather, volcanic mountains reaching well over 3,000m, and a concentration of altitude training terrain that draws professional teams and serious amateurs alike, in every month of the year.

Mount Teide, Tenerife

Spain's highest peak at 3,715m, Teide dominates Tenerife's cycling reputation, offering one of the longest continuous paved climbs in Europe — riders can climb from sea level to well over 2,000m on a single mountain, through changing vegetation zones from banana plantations near the coast to the bare volcanic landscape of Teide National Park higher up.

Why the Canaries Work Year-Round

Positioned off the coast of North Africa despite being Spanish territory, the Canary Islands enjoy a genuinely mild, stable climate throughout the year — this is precisely why professional teams use Tenerife specifically for altitude training camps at any point in the season, not just as a winter-only destination the way Mallorca or Calpe function.

Beyond Tenerife

Gran Canaria offers its own substantial climbing terrain, with a more compact but similarly mountainous interior, while Lanzarote and Fuerteventura trade serious climbing for flatter, wind-exposed volcanic terrain popular with triathletes for exactly that reason.

The Volcanic Landscape

What sets Canary Islands climbing apart visually is the volcanic terrain itself — stark, otherworldly landscapes on the higher slopes of Teide in particular, a genuinely different visual experience from Alpine or Mediterranean hill climbing elsewhere in our portfolio.

Altitude Training Considerations

Because Teide's climb genuinely reaches significant altitude, riders should be aware of the physical effects of elevation on performance — pacing needs adjusting on the upper slopes, and this is worth factoring into expectations if you haven't ridden at genuine altitude before.

Best Time to Ride

Genuinely rideable year-round, which is the whole point — winter offers a mild escape from colder European weather, while summer avoids the extreme heat found in some Mediterranean destinations, tempered by the islands' Atlantic position.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

Our Tenerife cycling tour is built around Teide's volcanic climbing and the island's genuinely reliable year-round weather, offering a training-camp-caliber experience without needing to time your trip around a specific season.

If you'd like to explore Gran Canaria or combine multiple islands in a single trip, we're also happy to design a fully custom tour around the wider Canary Islands for your group.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Mount Teide difficult for someone who hasn't ridden at altitude before?
The altitude itself does add genuine difficulty on the upper slopes, so pacing conservatively and expecting a harder effort than the gradient alone would suggest is important for first-timers.

Which Canary Island is best for serious cycling?
Tenerife stands out for Teide's singular climbing experience and its established training-camp reputation; Gran Canaria offers a strong, slightly more compact alternative.

Why do professional teams specifically choose the Canary Islands?
The combination of genuine high-altitude terrain and reliably mild, stable weather year-round is difficult to match elsewhere in Europe, making it uniquely suited to altitude training regardless of season.

Is this a good destination outside of a specific season?
Yes — this is one of its defining strengths compared to our other destinations, most of which have a clearer optimal season.

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours

title.raw: Cycling the Azores: Portugal's Volcanic Hidden Gem
title.rendered: Cycling the Azores: Portugal’s Volcanic Hidden Gem

content.raw:
If you want to know what genuinely undiscovered cycling terrain looks like in Europe, the Azores are a strong answer. This remote Portuguese archipelago in the mid-Atlantic offers volcanic mountains, crater lakes, and lush green landscapes found nowhere else on our roster, with a level of solitude on the road that's become increasingly rare across the rest of Europe.

What Makes the Azores Different

Unlike the sun-baked Mediterranean character of most of our island destinations, the Azores are genuinely green year-round, shaped by an Atlantic climate that keeps the volcanic landscape lush rather than dry — closer in feel to Ireland's wild character than to Mallorca or Sardinia, but with proper volcanic mountain terrain layered on top.

The Islands

The archipelago spans nine islands, with São Miguel, the largest, offering the most developed cycling infrastructure and terrain, including climbs around the dramatic Sete Cidades twin crater lakes and the volcanic Furnas valley, famous for its natural hot springs and geothermal cooking pits.

The Terrain

Riding here means genuine climbing through volcanic landscape — winding roads through dense, humid forest, past crater lakes, and along dramatic coastal cliffs, all on an island small enough to feel intimate but varied enough that no two days look alike.

Weather Considerations

The Azores' Atlantic position means changeable weather similar in character to Ireland — mild temperatures year-round, but genuine rain is common regardless of season, and packing for variable conditions matters more here than in our drier Mediterranean destinations.

Why This Appeals to Adventurous Riders

The Azores suit cyclists who've done the more established European destinations and want somewhere genuinely different — fewer other visiting cyclists, a distinct volcanic landscape, and a slower, more remote island pace of life than almost anywhere else in Portugal or the wider Atlantic.

Best Time to Ride

May through September offers the most reliable conditions, though "reliable" here still means packing for rain — the islands' mild, humid Atlantic climate doesn't follow the same dry-summer pattern as mainland Portugal or the Mediterranean.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

The Azores represent one of our more adventurous, off-the-beaten-path additions, offering genuinely unique volcanic scenery and a level of solitude on the road that's increasingly hard to find in more established European cycling destinations.

If you'd like an itinerary focused on São Miguel or want to explore multiple islands within the archipelago, we're also happy to design a fully custom tour around the Azores for your group.

Frequently Asked Questions

How does the Azores' climate compare to mainland Portugal or the Algarve?
Considerably wetter and greener year-round, closer in character to Ireland's Atlantic climate than the Algarve's dry Mediterranean-adjacent conditions.

Which Azores island is best for a first cycling visit?
São Miguel, the largest and most developed island, offers the widest range of established cycling terrain and infrastructure for a first trip to the archipelago.

Is this a good destination for riders seeking quiet, less-crowded roads?
Very much so — this is one of the Azores' defining appeals, with considerably less cycling tourism traffic than almost any other destination in our portfolio.

Do I need to pack differently for the Azores than for Mediterranean destinations?
Yes — pack for genuine rain regardless of season, similar to preparation for our Ireland tour, rather than assuming consistently dry Mediterranean-style weather.

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours

title.raw: Cycling the Austrian Alps: Grossglockner and Beyond
title.rendered: Cycling the Austrian Alps: Grossglockner and Beyond

content.raw:
Austria doesn't get quite the same attention as its Alpine neighbors France and Italy in cycling circles, but the Grossglockner High Alpine Road alone is reason enough to visit — one of the most spectacular high-mountain roads in Europe, built specifically as a scenic route rather than a simple point-to-point pass.

The Grossglockner High Alpine Road

Unlike most Alpine passes, which developed as practical trade or military routes, the Grossglockner was purpose-built in the early 1930s specifically as a tourist road, and it shows — sweeping, beautifully engineered switchbacks climbing to over 2,500m at the Hochtor pass, with the Grossglockner itself, Austria's highest mountain at 3,798m, dominating the view throughout. A toll road, it's exceptionally well maintained, with multiple viewpoints and a dedicated glacier-viewing spur road (the Edelweissspitze detour) adding extra climbing for those wanting more.

Why This Climb Is Different

The purpose-built, tourism-focused history of the Grossglockner road means the gradient and engineering feel noticeably more considered than many older Alpine passes — consistently graded switchbacks rather than the occasionally brutal ramps found on some historic French or Italian climbs, making it a genuinely spectacular but slightly more approachable high-mountain experience.

Beyond the Grossglockner

Austria's wider Alpine region offers considerably more than this single famous road — the Tyrol and Salzburg regions include numerous substantial passes and valley routes, generally quieter than equivalent terrain in France or Italy, with a distinctly Austrian character of well-kept mountain villages and excellent cycling infrastructure.

Weather and Season

As with any high Alpine pass, the Grossglockner is only open seasonally — generally May through October, with exact dates depending on snowfall — and conditions at the Hochtor summit can shift quickly regardless of valley weather, so the same packing advice as other high Alpine climbs applies here.

Austrian Mountain Culture

Austria's Alpine villages have a well-established tourism infrastructure built initially around hiking and skiing, which translates well to cycling visitors — excellent accommodation, genuinely good food (expect hearty Alpine fare alongside more refined options), and a level of polish to the whole experience that some riders specifically seek out.

Best Time to Ride

June through September offers the most reliable conditions, with July and August seeing the most tourist traffic on the Grossglockner road specifically, given its dual status as both a cycling destination and a popular scenic drive for general tourists.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

The Grossglockner and wider Austrian Alps work well as a distinctive addition to our Alpine offerings, or as one stage within a longer custom Raid Alps traverse linking Austria with neighboring Alpine regions.

If you'd like a dedicated trip focused on the Grossglockner and Tyrol region, we're also happy to design a fully custom tour around Austria for your group.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Grossglockner road busy with car traffic?
Yes, particularly in July and August, given its popularity as a scenic drive beyond just cycling tourism — earlier starts help avoid the busiest midday traffic.

How does the Grossglockner compare to the Stelvio or Galibier in difficulty?
Broadly comparable in altitude and length, though the purpose-built, consistently engineered switchbacks generally make for a slightly less punishing gradient experience than some historic Alpine passes.

Is there a toll to ride the Grossglockner road?
Yes, it's a toll road, though cyclists typically pay a reduced rate compared to vehicles — worth confirming current pricing when planning a visit.

Can the Austrian Alps be combined with neighboring regions like Slovenia or Switzerland?
Yes, this is a natural custom-tour combination given the geographic proximity, particularly appealing for a longer Raid Alps-style traverse.

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours

content.raw:
Italy is where I learned to race, and it's still the country I know better than any other on two wheels. The honest challenge isn't finding good riding here — it's narrowing down which region actually fits what you want from a trip, since "cycling in Italy" can mean anything from Giro d'Italia mountain passes to flat gravel through olive groves to an active volcano. Here's how I'd break it down.

Why Italy Works So Well for Cycling

Few countries pack this much variety into one place — genuine high-mountain climbing in the north, gravel and hill-country riding through the center, and flat, sun-baked coastal terrain in the south, all connected by a cycling culture that runs deep. This is the birthplace of the Giro d'Italia, and in the mountain regions especially, you're riding roads that carry real racing history, often with faded fan graffiti from the last time the Giro passed through.

Northern Italy: The Mountains

This is where Italy's biggest climbing reputation comes from, and it's split across a few distinct areas worth knowing apart.

The Dolomites offer the country's most photogenic high-mountain scenery — pale limestone peaks, Giro d'Italia climbs like Passo Giau and Passo Pordoi, and a season that runs roughly June through September. See our Dolomites timing guide for the details on when to go.

The Italian Alps, centered on the legendary Passo dello Stelvio, sit just west of the Dolomites and offer Italy's single most famous climb — full details in our Stelvio Pass guide.

Lake Garda gives you a different kind of northern riding entirely — lakeside roads, Valpolicella wine country, and the option to add the Stelvio as a day trip on our September departure. Read more in our Lake Garda guide.

Lake Como, further west, offers its own dramatic alpine-lake scenery and access to climbs used in the professional Il Lombardia race each autumn.

Central Italy: Hills, Gravel, and History

Tuscany is where central Italy's cycling reputation is built, and it splits into two genuinely different experiences worth understanding separately. The famous Strade Bianche white roads near Siena are ridden on a road bike and are the site of the professional one-day race held every March — see our Strade Bianche guide. For a longer, more varied gravel experience covering considerably more of the region on a dedicated gravel bike, our Tuscany Gravel Tour, based on the Tuscany Trail, goes further afield into the Apuan Alps foothills and the wilder Maremma.

For riders wanting to link the north and center of the country into one continuous journey, our Italy coast-to-coast guide covers a Tyrrhenian-to-Adriatic crossing through the central Apennines.

Southern Italy and the Islands

The south offers a completely different character from the mountainous north — flatter terrain, more intense sun, and a slower, more agricultural pace of life.

Puglia, Italy's flat southern heel, is our most approachable Italian destination — olive groves, whitewashed trulli architecture, and long, easy-paced riding days. Details in our Puglia guide.

Sicily brings genuine mountain climbing back into the picture, via the singular experience of riding the lower slopes of Mount Etna, an active volcano — see our Sicily guide.

Sardinia offers a wilder, more sparsely populated alternative — granite mountains in the interior and dramatic, quiet coastal roads, covered in our Sardinia guide.Frequently Asked Questions

How to Choose a Region

If climbing legendary Giro d'Italia passes is the priority, go north — the Dolomites or Italian Alps. If you want gravel and wine country at a gentler pace, Tuscany. If you want an easy, food-focused trip with minimal climbing, Puglia. If you want something genuinely unusual, Sicily's volcano or Sardinia's quiet granite interior. And if you can't choose just one, a coast-to-coast custom itinerary lets you experience more than one character of Italian riding in a single trip.

Best Time to Visit, By Region

Northern mountain regions need the June-to-September window when high passes are open. Tuscany and central Italy are best in spring (April-May) and autumn (September-October), avoiding summer heat. The south — Puglia, Sicily, Sardinia — follows the same spring/autumn logic, since summer heat here is often even more intense than further north.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

Between our standard departures and custom itineraries, we cover the full range of Italian riding described above. If you're not sure which region fits your group best, tell us what you're after — serious climbing, gravel and wine country, or an easier coastal pace — and we'll point you to the right fit, or design a fully custom tour that combines more than one region.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which Italian region is best for a first-time visitor?
This depends entirely on what you want — Tuscany offers the most balanced introduction to Italian cycling culture, scenery, and food for a first trip, while the Dolomites suit those specifically chasing serious mountain climbing.

Can I combine northern mountains with southern coastal riding in one trip?
Not easily in a single standard tour given the distances involved, but a custom itinerary can be built to visit more than one region if your timeframe allows.

Is Italy suitable for a mixed-ability group given the range of terrain?
Very much so — this is one of Italy's real strengths as a cycling country, since the range from Puglia's flat roads to Dolomites climbs means almost any fitness level has a well-suited regional match.

What's the single most iconic Italian climb to put on a cycling bucket list?
The Passo dello Stelvio is the classic answer — Italy's highest paved pass and one of the most famous climbs in the sport, detailed in our dedicated guide.

— Matteo Cigala

title.rendered: Cycling in France: The Complete Regional Guide

content.raw:
France is the birthplace of the Tour de France, and it shows in the riding — nearly every major mountain region here carries genuine racing history, often more concentrated and better signposted (literally, with painted road markers on the most famous climbs) than anywhere else in Europe. Here's how the country breaks down for cycling purposes.

The French Alps

This is France's headline cycling region, and rightly so — home to some of the most famous climbs in the sport. Alpe d'Huez, with its 21 numbered hairpins each bearing a stage winner's name, is covered in full in our Alpe d'Huez guide. The Col du Galibier, one of the highest and most frequently used Tour de France passes, gets its own detailed breakdown in our Galibier guide. Both are centerpiece climbs on our French Alps cycling tour, which bases you in the region for a week built around this kind of legendary climbing.

The Pyrenees

France's other great mountain range runs along the Spanish border, offering a wilder, quieter character than the Alps — narrower roads, more livestock sharing the tarmac, and climbs like the Col du Tourmalet that carry just as much Tour de France pedigree as their Alpine counterparts. Our Pyrenees climbing guide breaks down routes by difficulty level, from the approachable Col d'Aspin to the demanding Col du Portet. For riders wanting the ultimate regional challenge, we also cover the Raid Pyrénées — the classic coast-to-coast traverse of the entire range — as a custom tour option within that same guide.

Corsica

Technically part of France, but culturally and geographically distinct enough to deserve its own mention — this Mediterranean island packs genuine high-mountain terrain, reaching over 2,700m at Monte Cinto, into a compact island setting where dramatic granite peaks drop almost directly into the sea. Full details in our Corsica guide.

How to Choose a French Region

If you want the single most concentrated dose of Tour de France history, the French Alps around Alpe d'Huez and the Galibier is the classic choice. If you'd prefer quieter roads with equally serious climbing, the Pyrenees is genuinely underrated by comparison. And if you want mountains and Mediterranean coastline in one place, Corsica is unlike anywhere else on our roster.

Best Time to Visit

Both the Alps and Pyrenees need the June-to-September window when high passes are clear of snow, with July and August being warmest but busiest. Corsica follows a similar pattern, though its lower-elevation coastal sections are rideable slightly earlier and later in the shoulder seasons.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

Between our standard French Alps and Pyrenees tours and our custom Raid Alps and Raid Pyrénées options, we cover the full range of what French mountain cycling has to offer. If you're weighing the Alps against the Pyrenees, or want to build a longer trip linking multiple French regions, we're happy to design a fully custom tour around it.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which is harder, the French Alps or the Pyrenees?
Broadly comparable in overall difficulty — the Alps tend to have the highest single passes, while the Pyrenees' climbs are often just as demanding due to their steepness and length, with a wilder, less-manicured character.

Is Corsica considered part of "mainland" French cycling culture?
Geographically it's an island in the Mediterranean, but administratively and culturally it's French, while maintaining a strong distinct regional identity and language of its own.

Can I ride both the Alps and the Pyrenees on one trip?
Not within a single standard week given the distance between them, but a custom itinerary can link the two regions if your timeframe allows, or you could visit each on separate trips.

What's the single most famous French climb to put on a cycling bucket list?
Alpe d'Huez is the most internationally recognized, thanks to its numbered hairpins and frequent Tour de France mountaintop finishes, though the Galibier and Tourmalet both have equally strong claims among serious cyclists.

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours

title.rendered: Cycling in Spain: The Complete Regional Guide

content.raw:
Spain has quietly become one of European cycling's most important countries — not just for racing, but for where professional riders actually train and, in a lot of cases, live. Here's how the country's cycling geography breaks down.

Mallorca

The original winter training-camp island, Mallorca combines genuinely serious mountain climbing in the Serra de Tramuntana range with reliably mild off-season weather that draws professional teams every winter and spring. The famous Sa Calobra climb, with its 270-degree "tie knot" hairpin, and the longer Puig Major are both covered in our Mallorca guide.

The Costa Blanca (Calpe)

Mainland Spain's answer to Mallorca, the Costa Blanca around Calpe offers similarly mild winter weather and genuine climbing, centered on the popular Coll de Rates, but with more extensive inland terrain than an island setting allows and generally fewer other cyclists on the roads. Full details in our Calpe guide.

Girona

Less a training-camp destination and more the adopted home of professional cycling itself — an extraordinary concentration of professional riders lives in and around this Catalan town, drawn by good weather, varied terrain, and genuine cycling culture built up over more than a decade. Our Girona guide covers the local climbs, the Costa Brava coastal option, and what makes the town's cycling scene so distinctive.

Why Spain Works So Well for Winter and Shoulder-Season Riding

All three of these regions share a common thread — genuinely mild winter and early-spring weather that makes them natural complements to Alpine and Pyrenean destinations, which are closed under snow during exactly the months Spain is at its best. Building a season around Alpine summers and Spanish winters is a pattern a lot of our regular guests have settled into.

How the Three Regions Differ

Mallorca offers the most concentrated, internationally famous climbing within a compact island setting. Calpe trades some of that fame for more extensive mainland terrain and quieter roads. Girona offers the least singularly dramatic climbing of the three, but the richest cycling culture — café stops with actual professional riders, and a genuinely lived-in cycling town rather than a seasonal training destination.

Best Time to Visit

October through April across all three regions, avoiding the intense summer heat that makes serious climbing considerably less comfortable — this inverse seasonality compared to the Alps and Pyrenees is precisely what makes Spain such a valuable addition to a year-round cycling calendar.

How This Fits Into a Cigala Cycling Tour

Between Mallorca, Calpe, and Girona, we offer three genuinely different flavors of Spanish cycling, all suited to filling the winter and shoulder-season gap left by our higher-altitude destinations. If you're deciding between them, or want to combine more than one region in a single trip, we're happy to design a fully custom tour around it.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which Spanish region is best for a first winter training trip?
Mallorca is the most established and internationally recognized option, with the widest range of accommodation and cycling infrastructure built specifically around visiting training cyclists.

Is Girona worth visiting if I'm not chasing serious climbing?
Yes — its appeal is as much about atmosphere and terrain variety as pure climbing difficulty, making it a good fit for riders wanting a well-rounded trip over one built purely around a single famous climb.

Can I combine Mallorca and Girona in one trip?
Not easily within a single standard week given the travel between them, but a custom itinerary can link both if your schedule allows for a longer Spanish cycling trip.

Why do so many professional cyclists specifically live in Girona rather than training elsewhere?
A combination of good weather, varied terrain, a nearby international airport, and an early wave of resident professionals that snowballed into today's concentrated cycling community — practical reasons more than any single dramatic climb.

— Matteo Cigala
Former European Gran Fondo Champion, Vice World Gran Fondo & Gravel Champion, Italian Gravel Champion, Coach & Tours Director of Cigala Cycling Tours
